speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it occurs very rarely in the life of a nation that the courageous spirit of one person unites all the people in the celebration of his life, and in the mourning of his death. Such
Tributes to the late Terry Fox
a man was Terry Fox, whose death yesterday at the age of 22 has touched all of us with a sense of personal loss.
Canadians wanted desperately for Terry to live, to win his personal battle against the ravages of cancer. Yet it does not occur to any of us to look upon his death as a defeat or a failure. The reason, of course, is that we do not think of this remarkable young man as a victim, but as a victor. We do not think of him as one who was defeated by misfortune, but as one who inspired us with his example of the triumph of the human spirit over adversity.
When Terry lost a leg to cancer in 1977, he must have been sorely tempted to give up on life, to sink into the depths of self-pity and despair. Who among us could say that, in similar circumstances, we would not have done exactly that? Learning to walk again, after such a soul-searing shock, would have been remarkable enough. But Terry went beyond the merely remarkable, and gave new meaning to the word magnificent. [Translation]
Terry Fox chose to react most audaciously to his personal misfortune. He chose to set for himself a challenge which even our best athletes would likely consider to be beyond their ability. He decided not to walk but to run, and not only to run but to run across a continent. And he decided to do all that not for his own satisfaction but to bring hope and help to others.
For the magnitude of his courage and of the task he accomplished, we pay him tribute and quite rightly consider him as a hero. For the way he was able to inspire the country, we will be grateful forever to him. Terry did not complete his marathon of hope. He left us a part of it so that we may run it together. Let us get down to that task, while keeping in mind the example of a young man who devoted all his energy to that noble and generous objective-to spare others cancer, or at least to give them a better chance of recovering from it.
Let us keep fresh in our minds his example of boundless hope and courage. To that end the Government of Canada will establish the Terry Fox Humanitarian Award program, an endowment fund which will finance scholarships for some 250 young Canadians each year.
The program will give help and encouragement, in Terry's name, to young people who are pursuing excellence in their academic studies in the fields of fitness, health and amateur sport, or in fields related to community service. That will be one way of keeping the spirit of Terry Fox alive in our land, one way of remembering a young Canadian who gave far more to his country than his country was able to give to him.
In the midst of mourning, let us also celebrate the inspiring life of one who has touched all our lives and enriched all our lives.
I know, Madam Speaker, that all hon. members would want you to convey to Terry's parents and his family the profound sympathy of the House of Commons. But I also believe we
11022

June 29, 1981
Tributes to the late Terry Fox
want you to express to them more than our sympathy. We would like you to express as well our profound gratitude for the gift which Terry gave to all of us, the gift of his own boundless courage and hope, the gift of his magnificent and unselfish generosity, the gift of a life which has inspired us all.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to join the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in expressing both the deepest sympathy and the deepest gratitude of this House and the Canadian people to the family of Terry Fox.
I think some images last forever in our memory. None of us who saw it will ever forget that one young man, running alone against impossible odds; running, because quitting was no part of Terry Fox. He called his run the Marathon of Hope, and it did bring hope to millions of people who have battled cancer or other disease, or who have battled despair. But, Madam Speaker, hope was the result. The cause, the essence of the man we mourn, was courage. He ran alone and proved to all of us who have lesser troubles that one individual, alone with his will, can change our world. He did what Parliaments and philosophers talk about, and he enlarged the lives of everyone who knew his story.
[ Translation]
I know that today all Canadians mourn together for the death of Terry Fox, a son of whom Canada can be proud. He led a long and hard fight against death, and his courage will remain a great source of inspiration for all those who have to cope with illness or fear. Terry has done more things during his short life than most of us ever do in many more years.
[DOT] (M20)

Terry Fox was a Canadian hero whom the youngest children could understand. Yesterday morning he lost one battle, but his life was a victory, a victory of hope, of courage, of example. I pray that we in this Parliament and this country may be worthy of the standard of Terry Fox.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I am honoured to have the privilege of associating the members of the New Democratic Party with the tributes which have been given so eloquently by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).
We are all deeply conscious of what a hero Terry Fox has become in the life of this country. There seems to be a bit of significance in the fact that this man, though most of what he did was done last year, has in this International Year of the Disabled become such a hero. Indeed, he has shown by his courage and his determination that there are many disabled and afflicted people who are prepared to try to turn disability
or affliction into a challenge to the spirit. We believe this young man has done that for all of us.
Death is always hard to take or hard to understand. It is not so difficult when many years have been lived, but when it comes at such a young age it is very hard to take. Even so, as those who spoke before me have said, who could live a more creative, a more successful and a more effective life than Terry Fox has lived in the few years he has been on Canadian soil? We pay our deepest respects to him and to his memory.
There are times when older folk are inclined to wonder whether the younger generation has what it takes to carry on and build a better world. No one in Canada is saying anything like that today. If the generation between the ages of 20 and 30 can produce a Terry Fox, the future of this land is in good hands.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-COMPARISON WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Today it was announced that Canada has the highest rate of inflation of all industrialized countries in the world with the exception of Italy. Our inflation rate today is well above the average for industrialized countries, but of greater concern is the fact that it is about 2.5 percentage points higher than that of the United States, whereas a year ago we were three percentage points below the United States. Thus there has been a deterioration of about 5.5 per cent.
Has the government undertaken any studies of the performance in the United States to see whether we in Canada can learn anything to improve our performance?

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-COMPARISON WITH UNITED STATES

speechtext:
Madam Speaker,
1 was using a longer term than the minister. I was talking about a full year's experience where we have seen a very major deterioration. It is not who is playing with the numbers; it is he.
One of the major causes of the deteriorating performance in Canada relative to the United States is the inflationary expectations which are much more prevalent here than in the United States. We see that in the differential in wage negotiations and also in the wide spread between borrowing costs for long-term borrowers in the two countries.
My question is directed either to the minister or the Prime Minister. Is the government considering any new policies to broaden the battle against inflation so that it is not just a monetary or high interest rate policy, but a broader package of policies which would give Canadians the confidence that something is being done up here to fight inflation, similar to the package which was developed in the United States? If a package is not developed here, the credibility of the government will stay where it is now, that is, nil.

Madam Speaker, I am very glad that the hon. member has stressed in his preamble that inflationary expectations are more prevalent in Canada than in the United States. He is well aware that those inflationary expectations must be checked if both the monetary and the fiscal policy of the government are to be effectively supported. However, I would point out to him that these inflationary expectations are often fed by the comments made by his colleagues when they talk about interest rates or other effects of inflation. I would also like to remind him that, in the October budget, the Minister of Finance undertook to reduce government spending and the government deficit. These commitments support the monetary policy advocated by the Bank of Canada, and if we succeed in putting a stop to these inflationary expectations, these measures combined together will help us reduce in the middle term the inflationary pressures in Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Given the fact that the minister's special assistant met with the mayors of Ancaster and Glanbrook in my riding last week on the subject of compensation for property owners adjacent to the expanded Hamilton Civic Airport, and since those people who will be drastically affected appeared before an official expro-
Oral Questions
priation hearing all last week, is the minister now in a position to say what possible compensation will be available to those who could be really badly hurt by this airport expansion?

subsubtopic: HAMILTON CIVIC AIRPORT EXPANSION-COMPENSATION TO PROPERTY OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the answer is none. When the decision was made to expand the airport at Hamilton, it was known that the runway would have to be extended. This has affected a number of houses located nearby, and 16 or 17 houses are now being expropriated. A number of houses-possibly 80-will be affected noisewise. The answer in that regard is that, first, the noise effect will not be substantial and, second, there is no policy for expropriation of houses in the situation where noise has an effect.

Madam Speaker,
I have a supplementary question. Given the fact that many of these people bought their land before the airport was developed, could the minister not assure my constituents that his department will update the policy to take into consideration the injurious effects on the people? Will the minister judge the Hamilton airport situation on its own merits as a unique situation, and not ask the people to bear the cost of something which benefits the whole region? In short, will he listen to the concerns and the representations made by the people at the expropriation hearing?

Madam Speaker, I have in mind, as I am sure the hon. member does, the very strong representations which were made to me a few months ago before a decision with respect to the extension of the Hamilton airport was made. The hon. member was one of those who pressed me so hard I could barely stand up straight!
This is a policy which has been reviewed a number of times, that is, of no compensation for noise. I repeat that the noise factor in this instance is not of a considerable nature. If the department does not have a policy of compensation for the effects of noise, it is simply because of the consequences of creating a precedent. We would obviously have to revise our position for every airport in Canada. This is a position which we cannot sustain, unfortunately. I regret that.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Perhaps he will answer; I am not sure.
Over the weekend the government announced that it was withdrawing from the International Whaling Convention. The Prime Minister and I have exchanged correspondence on this

June 29, 1981
Oral Questions
matter over the course of the last few months. I simply ask him why?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I quite honestly thought that was the thrust of many of the environmentalists supported by the hon. member, that is, the thrust of their wish.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Their what?
The thrust of their wish, their desire, their expectation, their hope.
Hear, hear!

We had the choice of either staying in the IWC and incurring the blame of environmentalists or of getting out, and now we fail to obtain the support of the hon. member. I think what is crucial to the understanding of this matter is that we are withdrawing as members but we will still be present as observers.
We are not ourselves a whaling nation. We will still be able to express whatever arguments we can to the commission. Simply put, we will not be a full member and, therefore, we will not be part of its decisions, of those nations which continue to be whaling nations and which, if I understand the hon. member's representations correctly, are catching too many whales for the good of the cetacean species.

Madam Speaker, since we are in fact dealing with the endangered species of whales, and since those nations which will remain on the commission, if every other nation took the same position which Canada has taken, will be whaling nations, which are the very people who are endangering the species, surely it would make more sense for the Canadian government to continue to sit at the bargaining table, to continue to have a vote and to continue to have an opportunity to influence the outcome, rather than to abdicate responsibility and ultimately destroy the entire species?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I remember using that argument myself, particularly in an exchange I had with the hon. member. But this did not result in the withdrawal of the pressure which he and other environmentalists were placing on us. We were being blamed for the decisions of whaling nations with which we did not agree. I repeat that is why we have given notice that within a year we will withdraw from the commission as a member but will continue to participate as an observer.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Given the fact that Canada's withdrawal from the IWC amounts to a shameful international cop-out,
and given the fact that our withdrawal from the IWC will seriously impair our ability to influence the two principal whaling nations, the U.S.S.R. and Japan, and since that will have serious consequences on our own ability to regulate the situation in our own waters where whales are destroying the gear of fishermen on the Atlantic coast, will the minister tell the House why Canada decided to withdraw? Is Canada prepared to reconsider this shameful international cop-out?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, when Canada first entered the International Whaling Convention in 1946 we were a whaling nation. But since commercial whaling was abolished by government order in Canada in 1972 our policy has been under constant review. In the last year we have had an intensive review of this question, and as a result of that we have decided to remain associated with the International Whaling Commission as an observer and in its scientific work, using its scientific conclusions and contributing to them but no longer being a formal voting member of that body. It seems to me this is perfectly consistent with our interest at the present time, which is that of a non-whaling country.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, given the fact that only two of the 25 signatories to the IWC have a commercial whaling operation and that if all other member countries were to follow the rationale of Canada there would be no international whaling convention, there would be no conservation, no control, surely Canada has a responsibility not only to preserve these magnificent animals but it also has a responsibility to our own fishermen. Given all of these facts, surely Canada has an obligation to remain a member of the IWC. Will the minister reconsider?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it seems to me our obligation is not to a convention but to the conservation of the species. We are living up to that obligation. We are continuing to work with the scientific division of the International Whaling Commission. We are continuing to offer them our support. We continue to urge that a larger whaling convention, and a better one, replace the 1946 convention. In all of these areas we are completely and fully involved. That is our obligation, one which we are fulfilling.

subtopic: STEPS TO PREVENT EXTINCTION OF WHALES
STEPS TO PREVENT EXTINCTION OF WHALES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Now that Canada has not only removed itself for all practical purposes from the International Whaling Commission but has also undermined that major international body by withdrawing in the fashion in which it did, would the minister tell the House, the people of Canada in particular, and conservationists and environmentalists around the world who are concerned about the fate of the whale, what specific steps the government
June 29, 1981

intends to take outside the International Whaling Commission to prevent the extinction of this important mammal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STEPS TO PREVENT EXTINCTION OF WHALES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I was not speaking of steps outside the whaling convention but of steps in accord with the International Whaling Commission and in accord with its scientific mandate and interest. We are continuing our association with that body. As I mentioned before, we are also continuing our interest in a large and better whaling convention which would replace the 1946 convention.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister. Surely he would admit that all the initiatives to which he has referred would be much more effective if Canada were a full member of the International Whaling Commission rather than a second-class member on the outside looking in. In view of that fact, would the minister share with Parliament and the people of Canada, upon whose advice did the government act to withdraw from the International Whaling Commission, thereby undermining this important international body? Is it not true that every single major environmental and conservation group in Canada has urged against the action which the government has now taken? How can the government justify such stupidity against expert opinion, both within government and outside it, including expert opinion from its own advisory committee on the subject of whaling?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as I have said, every year before the meeting of the International Whaling Commission we have a review of all aspects of the whaling problem, and of our continued participation. After last year's meeting we launched an intensive review within the government, and I am sure the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will join with me in assuming the responsibility for persuading cabinet, on the basis of advice from our own officials, to take this step after full consideration. At the same time we reiterated our determination to contribute to the conservation of the species.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL AID TO MUNICIPAL TRANSPORTATION IN MONTREAL REGION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Last Friday the minister met with his counterpart in Montreal and announced that the Canadian government would be contributing some $80 million to the upgrading of public transit in greater Montreal. Mem-
Ora/ Questions
bers representing that area, who have been working towards this end for the past ten to 12 years are of course overjoyed by this announcement. My question is as follows: will the provincial government act alone as project manager? What was the provincial share announced at the press conference? Will the federal government have some visibility as far as its share is concerned, since this money was collected from taxpayers all across Canada, or will all the merit, credit and visibility for this project be given only to the province, as is the case in all other cost sharing programs?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL AID TO MUNICIPAL TRANSPORTATION IN MONTREAL REGION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last Friday in Montreal I recognized the contribution of all those, either ministers or ordinary members of Parliament, who had taken part in the development of this project. The federal share of $80 million is made up of three components: $10 million from the CN, $30 million from UTAP, which is a federal program designed to assist the development of urban transportation in the provinces, and $40 million made up of special subsidies.
In view of this substantial contribution, the province and the Montreal Urban Community will now be responsible for developing the project. They will be project managers since they will be responsible for the operations as well as any deficit incurred. I strongly emphasize that the federal contribution is now paid out directly and I think that Montrealers will recognize that it is quite substantial. The federal money will be used strictly to put commuter trains back into operating condition. Any improvement, transformation or updating of equipment will be the responsibility of the Quebec government and of the Montreal Urban Community.

subtopic: FUTURE OF VIA RAIL PASSENGER ROUTES

speechtext: Why?

Madam Speaker, a few months ago my hon. friend had a piece of paper and he informed Canada of its existence. Madam Speaker, I am quite sure that when the government makes a

A very substantial investment has been made in plant and equipment under the original CBC host broadcast proposal. speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):

subtopic: PROCESSING OF APPLICATIONS MADE BY FOREIGN DOMESTICS

speechtext:

have left the House I will direct it either to the acting minister or to the Prime Minister, if I can get his attention.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Acting Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):

speakeroldname: Hon. Francis Fox (Secretary of State and Minister of Communications) moved
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
speechtext:
that Bill C-37, to amend the Holidays Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
He said: Madam Speaker, before I begin my speech I would like to echo the remarks expressed in the House earlier this afternoon by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the House leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Knowles), and extend my condolences to the family of Terry Fox.

I think we all know that Terry Fox's bravery and stamina have made an indelible impression on this country, and particularly on the youth of this nation. His deed and his name will live to inspire young Canadians. His courage knew no barriers and exceeded all bounds. I am honoured to have the opportunity on Friday to announce the opening of the Canada Youth Centre in Ottawa which will bear the name of Terry Fox. I can think of no name more appropriate for a Canadian youth centre than the name of a young Canadian who has shown so much courage and so much commitment to his country.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to bring to the attention of all members of the House the importance of Bill C-37, to amend the Holidays Act. The bill, as we all know, received first reading on June 19, 1980, just a little more than a year ago today.
As hon. members of the House know, many attempts have been made over the years to change formally the name of that special national day on our calendar when we as Canadians proudly celebrate the founding of our nation.
I do not want to give a detailed legislative history concerning the subject, but I would like to point out that since 1966 some 22 private members' bills have been introduced concern-
Hear, hear!

ing the name of our July 1 holiday. This underlines the continuing interest shown by numerous members of Parliament and governments over the years in changing the name of our national anniversary to reflect more accurately our true sense of national identity.
An act of Parliament in 1879, 12 years after confederation, first established July 1 as a legal holiday under the name of "Dominion Day". The word "dominion" was the term which had been adopted at the time of confederation, some say at the suggestion of Sir Leonard Tilley, to refer to the union of the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick into one political entity. The term, as we all know, was taken from Psalm 72:8 "He shall have dominion from sea to sea". In fact, the choosing of that psalm in 1867 showed a degree of optimism. It was to take many more years, the building of a great railway and the influx of thousands of new citizens from other lands before Canada could truly reach a mari usque ad mare.

Mr. Speaker, the word "dominion" has always created problems for us and they are rather well known. According to Grolier's Encyclopedia Canadiana, and I quote:
One of the difficulties it creates is that it has no satisfactory equivalent in French.
They indicate that over the past ten or twenty years people have had a tendency to avoid using it, opting instead for adjectives such as "federal" or "national".
Professor W. L. Morton shares that point of view. He states that "Dominion of Canada" is an historic expansion which does not mean much in English and even less in French when it is translated by "Puissance du Canada". According to Professor Morton, and I quote his translated opinion:
Failure to define precisely-and with the required solemnity-what was in gestation, namely a new country in the British Empire, was at the source of much confusion in the minds of Canadians.
The word "dominion" was used for the first time in 1867 to designate Canada. Before that it had been used for Virginia, then a British colony, which was described as a former dominion. After the birth of confederation, the British were to use it to designate New Zealand in 1907. And in the Statute of Westminster of 1931, that word applied all at once to Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, the Irish Free State and Newfoundland. The word "dominion", which seemed appropriate at the time of confederation, has certainly lost some relevance with the passage of time. Canada has changed drastically over the past 114 years. The same thing goes for the way Canadians look upon themselves.

Little more than a century ago, Canada had just begun to take its first faltering steps as a sovereign nation. Canada's national identity was only beginning to emerge. Our evolution has been from a colonial entity, part of a great and far-reaching empire, to a mature nation, a mature nation assuming an important place within the family of nations. We have, indeed,
Holidays Act
come a long way from what Sir John A. Macdonald referred to as "a subordinate kingdom in the empire". Even that great empire from which we grew has itself evolved. Today that empire has become a Commonwealth of Nations, each equal in status.
This evolution, with respect both to Commonwealth members and to Canada in particular, has been a natural and progressive process. Moreover, a necessary part of this process has involved the reappraisal of the various symbols of our nationhood in order to ensure that such symbols properly reflect our attitudes and collective sense of identity as a sovereign and mature people.
Since the end of World War II Canada has steadily moved away from the word "dominion". This has not been motivated, as some may suggest, by a rejection of our heritage. Rather, it has been a manifestation of our need for a more modern and, perhaps more accurate description of our national self. Today Canadians see themselves not as citizens of a dominion-with its suggestion of control, dominance and colonialism-but as citizens of a proud and independent nation, Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Consequently, it is time, after 114 years of nationhood, to adopt for ourselves a truly Canadian day on which to celebrate, together, the anniversary of our nation's birth.
The name for this day must surely reflect the true nature of our collective identity. It must reflect the self-image which, I am sure all hon. members will agree, is already deeply and securely entrenched in the consciousness of today's Canadians. It must reflect, in a formal way, the consensus which exists across this land, reaffirming who we are and what we have become.
The annual observance of Canada's national day is a relatively recent phenomenon. Between 1868 and 1958 our national day was celebrated on precisely three occasions-once in 1868, again in 1917 marking the fiftieth anniversary of confederation and again in 1927 on the occasion of the sixtieth anniversary, or diamond jubilee, of confederation.
[ Translation]
Since 1958, Canada's national holiday has always been celebrated on Parliament Hill, except in 1976, when there were no great festivities to mark that day, even though there was a citizenship award ceremony. So we can say that since 1958, we have always celebrated our national holiday.

It has now become customary throughout Canada to talk of July 1 as "Canada Day". Indeed, the words "Canada Day" are used by literally millions of Canadians in all parts of the country in referring to our national day.
I think it would be fair to suggest that the word "dominion" means very little to present generations of Canadians to whom colonial days are past history. This is not a reflection on the words "Dominion Day" or on that honourable and historical

June 29, 1981
Holidays Act
title, "Dominion of Canada". The phrase "Dominion of Canada" has been a proud and worthy appellation but, as the Montreal Gazette said in an editorial on March 10 of this year, and 1 quote:
The word "dominion" does have a secure and honoured place in Canada's history. But not all historical labels remain accurate; this one certainly has not.
At the time of confederation the word "dominion" was hit upon as a new coinage to describe a country which was not, in fact, a sovereign state (as Canada was not in 1867).
But for the past 50 years Canada has been, in all but a narrow constitutional technicality... a truly independent nation. It should not retain a label which was coined to describe a colonial link.
Furthermore, "dominion" is not nearly as felicitous a word in French as in English. For French-speaking Canadians it is a verbal oddity which serves mainly to inflame old colonial wounds.
It is time to retire "Dominion Day" gracefully in favour of a name of July 1 which surely no one can find objectionable, Canada Day.
Surely it is time to call our national day by the name by which this country is recognized at home and abroad- Canada. Such recognition is in keeping with the growing sense of national consciousness shared by all Canadians.
Once again the Parliament of Canada is called upon to act on behalf of all citizens of this nation to change the official designation of Canada's most important national holiday. Will this call to action be answered, as in the past, by indecision? Will 1981 be added to the long list of dates whereon recognition of our national identity was once again proposed and once again denied? In proposing that the Holidays Act be amended to change "Dominion Day" to "Canada Day", Parliament is asked for no more than formalization of the consensus on this matter which already exists among the vast majority of the people of Canada.
Undoubtedly there will be some Canadians who will question or will even oppose such a change. It was not that long ago that similar concerns were voiced when proposals were brought forward to give Canada its own truly Canadian flag. Yet in the relatively brief period since its adoption by Parliament in 1964 our flag has become a proud and universally cherished symbol of our national identity.
On July 1, 1980 we proclaimed "O Canada" as our national anthem. Hon. members will agree with me that the adoption of national symbols is part of our growth process as a nation. The year 1981 could be the year we decide to make more relevant that one day of the year on which we celebrate the anniversary of Canada's birth.
This bill is representative of the pride we have in this great country called Canada. It is symbolic of the hope we have for the future of the Canadian people, the future which will be built by Canadians for Canada. It is fitting, therefore, that the special day on our national calendar when we Canadians proudly celebrate not only the founding and past of our nation but also the strength of its future should be called "Canada Day".
Undoubtedly there will be some hon. members who will speak in opposition to this bill.
You bet.
You can count on that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite say, "You bet". Their party has spoken of constitutional change and wants constitutional change to take place in Canada by consensus, but the refusal of some hon. members to make even the most minute change, such as changing the words "Dominion Day" to "Canada Day", is a clear indication of the attitude of some hon. members opposite which would see any kind of evolution in this country paralysed. I know that is not the general I attitude of hon. members opposite, but it surely is the attitude of some.
I call upon all hon. members of this House to act, hopefully by giving approval to the proposal that henceforth July 1 be known and celebrated with pride by all Canadians as "Canada Day".
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of attention to the fitting and appropriate opening of the speech of the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) a few moments ago when he referred to Mr. Terry Fox, but I express a sense of true sorrow that in the latter part of his speech he departed from that magnificent view he has of a person who was a magnificent Canadian and sullied that view by an attempt-I think in the wrong way-to raise a sense of partisanship about an issue which is important to the country.
At the outset let me say that I associate myself completely with the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the words today of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the words of my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), about the importance to our country of the contribution which has been made by Mr. Fox to that sense of togetherness as a nation for which we all continue to strive. I applaud wholeheartedly and without reservation the steps the government has taken to establish in the name of Mr. Terry Fox a youth centre here in the national capital. I join with every Canadian in recognizing the appropriateness of Mr. Fox being named a member of the Order of Canada.
When the news of his death came on Sunday morning, it occurred to me that there was a sense of grief shared in this country in the same way and to the same degree that there was a sense of joy at his undertaking and the great success of his undertaking. It was grief over his being removed from this earth when he had made a contribution larger than anyone could make after a full life. Canada's birthday on July 1 will be dulled somewhat by the fact he will not be here to celebrate it with us.
That brings something else to mind. He has demonstrated, 1 think in a very humane, direct and understandable way, the importance of the concept that this country is greater than the sum of its parts, and that there is a depth of humanity, courage and determination in ordinary Canadians that sur-
June 29, 1981

prises us all from time to time. As Canadians we have a great duty to treat everything, including national symbols and their creation, with respect. I hope that will be the spirit of this debate as we talk about an important symbol, a name for a day.
I do not agree with Professor Morton who, in effect, said Dominion Day is only an historical term, with emphasis on "only". To many Canadians it is much more than that. I do not agree with those who say that the 22 private members' bills over the years, given the way they are dealt with in this House, is a way for us to consider and determine absolutely, without reservation, that the time has come to act. I intend to speak about that a little later.
However, the government has brought in a bill, the first time since I have been here that this matter has been dealt with as a government bill, and I intend to deal with it that way. The bill before us prescribes a change in the name of our national holiday which the government and many Canadians would like to see. Equally so, it is a change many Canadians do not want to see. This difference of views is one which the Parliament not only should but has a duty to consider carefully. We are not debating a law in the ordinary sense of defining a code of justice or a standard of behaviour; we are judging the patriotic response Canadians give to the long standing and legal name of our national holiday, Dominion Day, as contrasted with the proposed name Canada Day.
I believe that before we make this change the government must satisfy the House that the overwhelming majority of Canadians will respond enthusiastically. They must show there will not be millions of Canadians who will feel they were irrationally robbed of the benefits of an imaginative compromise reached by the Fathers of Confederation in 1867. It will not be enough to say that we are simply confirming current usage.
We all know the promotion of the change is government policy, and the name-in-waiting has been vigorously pushed through government usage and ad campaigns. Dominion Day is never mentioned. All around us the government's propaganda machine talks of Canada's day and sometimes, very daringly, of Canada Day.
We might ask: Why bother about the bill at all? The government has abandoned Dominion Day without legislation. Perhaps the legal change will save money by eliminating the need for a yearly advertising campaign. It is really right that the name Canada Day, reasonable as it may seem as a name for Canada's day, should be imposed by the government and its advertising? Must the answer to that question inevitably be yes? If it is to win the hearts and minds of Canadians, should it not emerge from Canadians themselves? Is it really proper to adopt the name by executive decision in majority vote without consulting Canadians themselves? Is it proper to drum it into the Canadian people as an accomplished fact by lavish advertising, and then introduce a bill on the pretence that everyone seems to want it anyway? Symbols of nationalism should emerge from the people. We should be sure that
Holidays Act
Canadians want this change before we impose it on them. Is it unreasonable to be sure before we act, Mr. Speaker?
According to the government the change is desirable for three reasons. First, Canadians use Canada Day all the time anyway. I suggest that even if Canadians feel uncomfortable with Dominion Day, it is reasonable to ask if a spontaneous cry has gone up for Canada Day across the nation. It is reasonable to suspect instead that it is part of a government inspired larger pattern over the past 15 years of putting "Canada" in front of, behind and on top of every agency, body, function or activity of government in this country.
What is wrong with that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Second, we are told it is perfectly natural to name the national holiday after the nation. Well, it may be natural but, oddly enough, it is not common around the world. I did a survey among Commonwealth nations. I have to tell my friends that Australia has called their holiday Australia Day since 1901. Apparently they have no hang-ups over that; it is their tradition.
However, New Zealand called their day Waitangi Day, or New Zealand Day synonymously. Quite a controversy surrounding the day has arisen in New Zealand because it commemorates the ceding of Maori lands to the British on February 6, 1840. The native people are very sensitive to the symbolism and the land issue there. When they tried to change it to New Zealand Day there was a great deal of protest. The preference of the majority is for Waitangi Day.
India has two national holidays. They call one Independence Day, August 14; and Republic Day on January 26, commemorating their constitution. In Nigeria, October 4 is National Day and it has never been called anything else. If you go to Great Britain, it is not called England Day, English Day or even United Kingdom Day. It is called St. George's Day. That happens to be a holiday when they do not close the shops or anything like that but they celebrate the great tradition of St. George. There is another day there called the Queen's birthday. It is not a holiday but it is celebrated on the closest Saturday to the Trooping of the Colour ceremony. So, Mr. Speaker, if the Secretary of State's argument is that it is traditional, I have to say with respect that he is wrong.
Then thirdly, Mr. Speaker, we are told that "dominion" conjures up the wrong spirit among Canadians, that there is something wrong with the word. There maybe something in that, and I will return to it in a moment. There are some good arguments for calling July 1 Canada Day. Whether or not the demand for the change is spontaneous, which I doubt, it is not inevitable that a country's holiday should bear the name of the country.
I have mentioned St. George's Day and the Queen's birthday. In France it is Bastille Day; in the United States it is Independence Day. There is a reason for those names. Each of those names in those countries evokes a moment of glory or a decision from the nation's past. It is a reason for a celebration.

June 29, 1981
Holidays Act
To say U.S. Day, England Day or France Day, would tell us nothing except that people are more likely to be at the beach than at home. Should we not consider whether Canada Day, instead of being inevitable and obvious, is perhaps somewhat sterile, neutral and dull?
And plastic.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps plastic. I wonder whether we have not finally satisfied the national mania for playing cute name games with the name of our country and threatening to kill our reverence for it by overuse. Things used to be described as they were. Now we sacrifice description in favour of making the obvious point that this is Canada. Obviously this is Canada.
We are no longer content to refer to the Department of Transport, the Bureau of Statistics or Dominion Day. It must be Transport Canada, Statistics Canada and Canada Day. I suspect somebody will bring in a proposal which will shock the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; they will call this place "Commons Canada". The hon. member for Mount Royal will be very fortunate if he does not become "Canada Prime". Perhaps the Secretary of State will become "Canada Sect State". I am glad he smiles. Let us seriously think for a moment whether we have not had enough of this cloying, homogenizing cuteness. Let us assume this year that we are Canadians and start describing things as they are.
It may be that the term "Dominion Day" leaves many Canadians unmoved or puzzled. We all know its origins in the Seventy-Second Psalm, as the Secretary of State said, and of Sir Leonard Tilley's imagination in choosing it as a replacement for the unacceptable word "kingdom", as part of a compromise at the beginning of the country in 1867. If we look at the meanings of "dominion" in the Oxford English Dictionary, we can see the problem. There are six different definitions, including one referring to its incorporation in key statutes here in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Read them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will. The first one is:
The power or right of governing and controlling; sovereign authority; lordship, sovereignty; rule, sway; control, influence.
This is the word "dominion" about which I am talking.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
speechtext: What is it in French?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is here a sense of someone controlling something. Since we do not wish to celebrate being controlled, obviously this definition is not the relevant one. The second one is:
The lands or dominions of the feudal lord.
This is unsuitable unless we accept the Prime Minister as a feudal lord. Perhaps some hon. members opposite accept him as a feudal lord.
A funeral lord.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Some would wish that he would be accepted as a funeral lord. The other part of that definition reads:
The territory owned by or subject to a king or ruler, or under a particular government or control.
This is obviously our sense of the word as Canadians. In fact the Canadian usage is the prime modern example given by the Oxford Dictionary for this meaning. This is how we use it, as Oxford defines it. The other meanings listed are: "ownership, property; right of possession" and "domination". I think they are also unsuitable.
Reading the usage of the word in the Oxford English Dictionary drives home a number of points. First, the word is no longer in common usage in most of its meanings. Second, most of the meanings refer to domination rather than freedom. Third, for its usage in the Canadian sense, Canada itself is listed as the example. It would not be surprising if many Canadians were unsure of the appropriation of the word as a description of a free and independent nation of the twentieth century. It ought not to surprise any of us.
Does it follow that our use of an unusual word should be ended? When Sir Leonard Tilley chose that word, he did what most of us do every day as politicians. He racked his brains and pulled out a word which allowed the Fathers of Confederation to reach a compromise. Perhaps it was the final compromise of three years of colonial diplomacy leading to confederation. It was a compromise which has not lost all of its validity, even if the word is more out of the ordinary now than it was then. It nicely describes our government as one grounded in the traditions of constitutional monarchy but separate and free. It recalls the Christian-Judean tradition which underlies the faith of our ancestors and much that is worth preserving in our present culture. Not least, its usage is identifiably Canadian. As a description of the legal and emotional basis of Canada, the word "dominion" has had meaning for Canadians for over a century.
The government would like us to believe that this is a simple housekeeping issue. Well, it is not. Hon. members opposite would have us believe that the name "Dominion Day" has no merit at all and that "Canada Day" is the natural replacement. I have tried to show why .1 believe the issue is not quite that simple. I wish it was, but it is not. Dominion Day may be confusing or outdated to some Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Obsolete.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Or obsolete to some Canadians, as my hon. friend says. But whether or not hon. members opposite like it, it is rooted in the history and traditions of Canada. Canada Day may appear patriotic and inevitable, but it does not tell us what it is about our country or its history that we are celebrating on that day. We are not celebrating the name; we are celebrating something much more profound. We are celebrating a concept.
A former member of the other place, Senator Eugene Forsey, said it best in a speech to the Men's and Women's Canadian Clubs of Edmonton on June 19, 1956. 1 think these
June 29, 1981

comments are worth while for every Canadian to remember when they are talking about the concept of what is embodied in Dominion Day or Canada Day, indeed in the country. The question put was: What do we celebrate? He answered it this way:
Dominion Day celebrates one of the greatest feats of modern history: the making of a new nation, and a new kind of nation, by a handful of people of differing origins, differing languages, differing creeds, differing histories and differing interests, and in the face of obstacles that might well have daunted the boldest and most resolute statesmen. Everything was against them. The country was huge; most of it was empty; the Americans were pressing in upon the territories of the Hudson's Bay Company, threatening to cut off the new Dominion from any expansion West or North. There was hardly any industry: manufactured goods came overwhelmingly from Britain, and to central Canada for five months of the year through American ports, so that at any moment the Americans could strangle the economic life of Ontario and Quebec.
Central Canada and the Maritimes knew little of each other, and many Maritimers feared "Upper Canadian" domination. Communications were poor: there was no railway from the Maritimes to central Canada, and, what was worse, the main central Canadian railway, the Grand Trunk, came in from the United States and went out into the United States. If the Fathers of Confederation had followed their economic interests, there would have been no Confederation. They would not have gone to Charlottetown, and from Charlottetown to Quebec. They would have gone to Washington, and asked to be let into the American Union.
Then something happened which he describes as "A Supreme Act of Faith". He said:
Confederation was a supreme act of faith, faith that defied geography, defied economics, defied the "manifest destiny" of the Americans to rule the whole continent from the Rio Grande to the North Pole.
Faith in what? In something beyond economics, beyond the material; faith that the British North American colonies had a heritage worth preserving, worth developing, worth paying an economic price for; faith that on this rock our people could build a great nation, part of a great Commonwealth.
We sometimes forget two of the basic things that mark Canada off from every other country in the Americas. First, she is the only American nation which has deliberately chosen not to break with its past, both French and British. The most important thing for Canadians about the American Revolution is that we refused to have anything to do with it. We deliberately chose to keep our roots and draw nourishment from them. Confederation reaffirmed that choice.
I believe in the spirit of those words. We owe it to the Canadians whom we represent to proceed thoughtfully. There is no need for sudden deadlines. Canada will be around, we all pray, for a long time.
This is not the first time the symbols of Canadian identity have been debated in this House. Perhaps we can learn a bit from the past debate. Even those of us who were not here at the time remember the anger and the acrimony of the flag debate. It all started reasonably sanely, with a committee examining several possibilities. At one time a flag was emerging. It had two blue bars and a red maple leaf. However, the emerging consensus was lost.
A second committee recommended the present flag and it was imposed by the government. It is not worth arguing as to whether our present flag is completely entrenched in our consciousness, but it is clear that in its early history a great deal of hostility had to be overcome, not just from those who preferred to salute the old flag, but from those who wanted the first new flag. Canadians have come to accept the maple leaf
Holidays Act
but not without a large commitment of funds for free flags, pins and advertising.
We have just finished almost all of the Constitution debate. Again a package has been imposed. Again many feel our best constitutional and legal traditions have been needlessly violated. Once again the public is being bombarded with advertising, to persuade it not only to embrace, but to demand, the new order. Even if the Supreme Court finds the package barely legal, lawyers will be fighting over the constitutional provisions for a generation.
Now Dominion Day is to become Canada Day, not by emergence or consensus, but by contentious legislation backed by clever advertising.
Next year, July 1, 1982, we could see the most absurd evidence of this wrongheaded approach to forging a national identity. On Canada Day, a name approved by this House over the objections of millions of Canadians, our national flag, created by this House over the objections of millions of Canadians, will be raised to salute our new Constitution- perhaps certified as barely legal after being guillotined through Parliament.
Is this creative nation-building? Is this the stuff of pride, partiotism and inspiration? Or is it the stuff of cynicism, manipulation and force?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is the stuff of Parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member opposite interrupts, but I will ignore him as usual. One paradox which may even strike the hon. member opposite if he is alert is that at next year's celebration the crowds will be singing our national anthem in two entirely different languages, with the English-language singers struggling to remember changes made in the wording of a song accepted in its old version for 50 years, and the other language group singing the version used for generations. But no one will be bitter; no one will feel frustrated and ignored.
Why? Because when we confirmed "O Canada" as our national anthem on June 27 last year and made some wording changes, we concluded a process which has been open and deliberate, a process which had been going on for a great many years involving this institution, and I think rightly so. That is why that bill passed last year in the way in which it did. That is why we had that marvellous ceremony on the Hill last July 1-because the evolutionary approach to national symbols had been utilized by the government. I pray it uses it with respect to all symbols.
We drew explicitly on the unanimous recommendations of a committee which reported on February 16, 1968, only three years after the destructive and acrimonious flag debate. Canadians had been heard. They agreed with the changes. There was little dissent and there is no bitterness. Every one of us who was here on that Friday afternoon rose and sang together, each in his own way, in his own language, but with the same feeling, the national anthem which had been proclaimed on that day. That is the model of co-operation we

June 29, 1981
Holidays Act
should look to. Our symbols of common nationhood should not be conceived in controversy and preserved to remind us of our quarrels. They should emerge from the spontaneous sentiment of Canadians and remind us of our common triumphs as a peaceful and productive people.
I suggest that this bill should not be passed-not right away, at least. We should send the subject matter to a committee, listen with respect to the views of Canadians, and then debate a new bill based on our conclusions. We may, after consideration, decide that we want "Canada Day". We may see the link to our history in "Dominion Day". We could opt for "Confederation Day" or "Dominion of Canada Day" or any other name evocative of a proud moment in our history.
I think it is important that we do this, and do it in the right way, having regard to the best traditions which we have established in this Parliament, the culmination of which took place prior to July 1, 1980.
I feel so strongly about the evolutionary approach to the development of national symbols that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after "that" and by substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-37 an act to amend the Holidays Act, be not now read a second time
but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the Standing Committee on
Communications and Culture."
It is important that we begin this process and carry this process the right way. I think this suggestion that I have made will satisfy most that the Parliament of Canada will not act precipitously, but, rather, will gather unto itself the views of Canadians so that we can have, at some day in the reasonably near future, the same kind of celebration and the same kind of proclamation with respect to the name which we would apply to July I in each year as we now use with respect to the National Anthem. This is the course of wisdom. I grant you, Mr. Speaker, it is not the course of speed, but it is the course of wisdom.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words today in support of changing Dominion Day to Canada Day. I do so by reflecting back a number of years ago and thinking of the words which were said in this House by the Conservative House leader, that we need an evolutionary approach toward changing national symbols. I happen to agree fully with the leader of the House for the Conservative party that we need an evolutionary approach. We need a national consensus. We need input from Canadians. We have to democratize this institution and other institutions of Canada so that ordinary people will have their voices heard.
I was speaking earlier this morning about that issue through the House leader of my party, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He reminded me that in the year I was born 1946, or perhaps 1947-
You are not sure when you were born?

-an hon. member of this House, a Mr. Cote from the riding of Matapedia-Matane, introduced a private member's bill to the House of Commons requesting that we change Dominion Day to Canada Day. Does Your Honour know what happened with the private member's bill some 35 years ago? It was passed by the House of Commons.
All three readings.
All readings in the House were passed by the House of Commons.
All in one day!

As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says, they were passed all in one day. Not only was the bill passed, with a few members perhaps objecting verbally as it went through, but it was passed unanimously, with all members of the Conservative party, the Liberal party, the CCF party in those days, the Social Credit party, supporting unanimously the private member's resolution to change the name of Dominion Day to Canada Day.
Does Your Honour know what then happened? The democratic process ended in the Senate and the Senate said "no" to changing the name of our day from Dominion Day to Canada Day.
Let us put Walter Baker in the Senate.

We had democracy thwarted in the Senate of Canada some 35 years ago.
I fully endorse the evolutionary approach to national symbols enunciated by the Tory opposition leader today. However, I think we have had that process. We went through all stages, except for the archaic Senate, in 1946 or 1947. I think that ever since then the overwhelming majority of Canadians I have met anywhere in the country have said to me, "Why do we not come into the modern era and change the name of our national day to Canada Day?" On behalf of our party, I want to plead strongly that cause with my friends in the Conservative party.
Hear, hear!

I also want to say that I recognize that some people, a very distinct minority of people in this country, now feel very strongly about Dominion Day, because Dominion Day for many people in this country symbolizes a link to the British past and to the British Commonwealth. I can say, as half of my family background came from England back in the early part of this century, that for many people that link is very important. I think a link has to continue with Britain and with the British Commonwealth. However, I believe we can do that in many other ways. I believe that changing the name of the day would not sever that relationship which is so important to many Canadians. I think that what it would do instead would be to allow Canadians of British ancestry to feel proud of Canada, along with people of French Canadian ancestry and people who come from other countries of the world which have no historic ties with either Britain or France. I believe it
June 29, 1981

is very important that all of us unite around this symbol, and this symbol is Canada Day.
I listened with interest as well to the House leader of the Conservative party when the spoke about "Why Canada Day?" In France, it is "Bastille Day", and not "France Day"; in Britain, it is "St. George's Day", and so on. I found his argument very interesting, except that I have searched my mind for an alternative but I do not really see any alternative.
I fear that perhaps someone might want to call it "Constitution Day" at some time.
"Trudeau Day".

"Confederation Day" was mentioned. One Liberal across the way mentioned "Trudeau Day". However, I think of all those alternatives. The only one in which there is a broad consensus across Canada is calling it Canada Day to symbolize the country from coast to coast.
Much has been said about the contribution which was made to this country by Terry Fox, his courage and vision. This was referred to as well both by the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) and the opposition House leader. I want to associate ourselves with that courage and vision which Terry Fox showed Canadians. I think he showed us a number of things; but one thing he showed us in his Marathon of Hope, the run from Newfoundland to British Columbia which, of course, he had to abandon about two-thirds of the way across the country, is that Canada is bound together by some pretty strong threads, and that we are all Canadians. Even though we are diverse and we have our disagreements, we are still all Canadians. I think that in honour of people like Terry Fox, the rest of us should stop arguing and bickering once we reach a major consensus, and at least agree very quickly on the bill which is before the House today.
The other thing I wanted to say, in conclusion, is that symbols are very important. The national flag of this country is very important and the National Anthem of Canada is very important. I think the name of Canada Day will be very important. However, even though these symbols are very important, it is crucial that we also try to define for ourselves what Canada really means. What kind of a country are we? What kind of a country do we want to become?
In the past our pioneers did very well in creating a country which was basically open, free and democratic. In doing this, they often sailed against the tide, they climbed many long hills, and many people fell by the wayside during those struggles. We have to pick up the torch of many of these pioneers and look back at what they practised. What they practised, when they spoke about Canada and dreamt about Canada, was a country which was built on co-operation, on sharing, on freedom and on democracy. What we should be doing in the future is instilling some of those principles in the Canada of tomorrow. Because I do not think we can build a Canada if we are going continuously to have confrontation after confrontation between various governments and regions. We have to recognize that this country is immensely diverse, that we can cherish that diversity, that we can have harmony in that
Holidays Act
diversity, that people are different one province from the other, and that in the modern world of today people are proud of their differences and their diversity.
In the modern world today people will be expecting to have more control over their own lives and to have a more democratic Canada-I mean that in the true sense of democracy- because I believe that in this country Parliament, or this government, and many other institutions are becoming less and less democratic. People are having less and less input over their lives. I think people are now demanding that they have more meaningful input over the direction of their country, that there be more localized democracy, that people's differences be allowed to flourish.
Are those differences we are developing a unique state called Canada? We are not the great melting pot the United States is to the south of us. We are not trying to create one Canadian from coast to coast who is similar and speaks the same language, who eats the same food, who goes to bed at the same time every night and who practises the same culture. We have to be proud of our differences, and we have many, many differences.
As well as being proud of our differences and diversities, when it comes to co-operation we have to learn more from the past and from our pioneers. Co-operation built this country in the early days. It was a dream of people working together. It did not matter whether they spoke the French language or the English language. Later on people from many lands, with diverse backgrounds co-operated in building a great state. We have to apply that principle to some of the complex problems that we are facing today, such as revenue sharing, energy and constitution building. These are the things that will cause us a great deal of strain in the next few years to which some of these principles should be applied.
Lastly I want to mention the principle of sharing. This country was also built on sharing. My own province of Saskatchewan in the 1930s and 1940s was almost bankrupt. Many of the things that were accomplished then were accomplished, in part, because of the sharing we had in this country. For example, we had an equalization plan, a Crowsnest Pass rate agreement which helped farmers to sell their grain at lower costs, and a Canadian price for oil so we could get a better price for the oil we produced. Some of these things helped to build my province and helped to build the west.
In the Canada of tomorrow, I think we will have to remember that we must continue to share so that we have equality of conditions in each and every province and each and every region. If we can do that, if we can recognize our diversity, allow it to flourish and to grow, then I think there will be less friction and fewer suspicions. If we can co-operate and work together, recognize that we are multicultural and a bilingual country, and combine that with a real sense of wanting to share things so that we can use some of the new found wealth in western Canada to help the Newfoundlanders and perhaps use some of the wealth that is still in Ontario to help people in

June 29, 1981
Holidays Act
the Atlantic provinces, then, in the long run, all of Canada will benefit.
Finally, we should be putting more emphasis and stress on making all of our institutions truly democratic so that Canadians from all walks of life have a real input into what Canada should be. If some of these things could be done, then perhaps some of the visions and the courage which Terry Fox had would, in the future, be rewarded with actual legislation in Canada.
Yesterday I happened to hear an open-line show which was discussing the impact Terry Fox had on this country. Many people said positive things about his courage, his determination, his spiritual and emotional strength. But one lady really summed it up by saying that this is all fine and well, but if we really want to do something for his memory, then legislators in this country should do something to solve some of the causes that he stood for.
I believe that in this House we can resolve some of the problems he stood for. We can do a lot more to bring Canada together and to unite this country. We could be putting more funds into things such as cancer research and aid to the disabled than we are. We could be building a Canada of hope for the future where everyone, regardless of one's background, would have a much fairer chance at an equal and happy life.

Mr. Speaker, may I also commence my remarks by adding my own word of distress at the news of the death of Terry Fox. If I can coin a phrase from my comrades in the legion, it is that "we shall not forget".
I am very proud to have the opportunity to speak today in support of Bill C-37, an act to amend the Holidays Act. This is a bill to officially entitle July 1 "Canada Day". Is it not strange that we should be debating such a bill 114 years after the original July 1 when our great country of Canada was born? I must admit that I always found it strange that July 1 could be called by any other name but Canada Day.
The House leader of the Official Opposition when speaking on this bill said there is no need for sudden deadlines. He said the bill should not be passed, not right away at least. He stated that we should not act precipitously. The Conservative party is, as usual, trying to have the best of both worlds. The Conservative party will not let the bill pass, but it will try to stay onside by suggesting that the subject matter be sent to a committee. In the nine years that I have been a member of this House, we have done just that, but to what avail? Let me put on the record today some of the events that have taken place.
As I said, I found it strange that we could designate July 1 by any other name but Canada Day. On October 15, 1974, I tabled Bill C-231 in this House for first reading. That bill came up for debate on March 14, 1975. At the end of the debate on March 14, 1975, the subject matter of the bill was referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. That bill was essentially the same bill as the one we are debating today, a bill to name July 1 Canada Day.
On October 14, 1975, the then secretary of state, the Hon. James Hugh Faulkner, said, as reported in Hansard at page 8158:
The government feels that the majority of Canadians accept the terminology Canada Day/Fete du Canada.
The subject matter of Bill C-231, to which I have referred, came up for discussion in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on Tuesday, February 24, 1976. Unfortunately, the opposition did not see fit to let a report come back to the House of Commons.
We tried again. On October 22, 1976, I introduced Bill C-373, an act to amend the Holidays Act, again in an attempt, if possible, to designate officially July 1 as Canada Day. That one did not go very far.
On December 21, 1976, the secretary of state introduced Bill C-30, with exactly the same intent. That bill was entitled "an act respecting certain holidays".
Still carrying on in the same effort to achieve one small step for Canada, we tried again on October 30, 1978, when we introduced Bill C-232, with exactly the same objective. The bill was entitled "an Act to amend the Holidays Act". This bill came up for debate on November 30, 1978. If I can quote one sentence from my remarks, as reported in Hansard at page 1669,1 said:
-what this bill seeks to do is regularize a situation which for all practical purposes is a fait accompli. In most parts of the country the July 1 holiday is at the present time designated Canada Day.
Bill C-232 arrived in the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration where it was debated on March 7, 1979. At the end of the debate it was finally reported back to the House. We now seemed to be making some progress. On March 13, 1979, one week later, in this House, I moved:
-that Bill C-232, to amend the Holidays Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, be concurred in.
That motion was agreed to, whereupon I then moved "that the bill be read the third time and do pass". Debate followed and members of the Official Opposition talked out the motion so that it could not be brought to a vote. So much for our House rules.
We tried again on May 2, 1980, when we inroduced bill C-201, an act to amend the Holidays Act. I wrote a note to the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox). I quote:
Attached is a copy of Bill C-201, an act to "legalize" the terminology "Canada Day". This Bill has been introduced in every Session in the last several years and has always been "talked out" by a half dozen Conservative MPs who are vehemently opposed to the change.
It should be recognized that even a government Bill brought before the House to achieve the same objective, cannot expect to be passed without closure or lengthy debate.
It is an example of the power of a very small minority that is able to block the passage of legislation that can obtain all-party support and would pass a House vote with an overwhelming majority.

popular, cultural and community activities ... Canada Day (would) be non-ideological.. . non-partisan and non-political.

The Government of Canada should undertake to create a Canada Day organization-

Early in the last great war I came to Canada to train as a pilot. After the war I returned with my family to settle in Canada. I chose Quebec. Despite all the economic and social turmoil in Quebec today, I do not regret that original choice and would very happily make the same decision again today. I am very proud to call Quebec my province. I am especially proud of the very warm reception that I always receive in the constituency of Vaudreuil, the region of Canada which I represent in this House. However, being a proud Quebecer makes me no less proud to wear a flag of Canada pin, to wave our Canadian flag, to sing our national anthem "O Canada" and to speak out loudly of this country, Canada, that surely is the finest country in the world in which anyone can live.
It saddens me that members of the official opposition try to hang on to the past instead of building with pride for the future. Fortunately their attempts to continue our colonial status are already doomed to failure. Those who hang on to their antiquated memories can talk out this bill, but I in company with a huge majority of the 24 million persons who proudly call themselves Canadians will sing loudly and proudly their national anthem "O Canada" on Wednesday of this week, July 1, 1981, Canada Day.

One thing we can say is that Canadians, unhappily after this last year, are more divided in terms of the symbols of the country than when we started this year. There is no doubt about that. So I question whether at this stage it is auspicious for us to add more to the whole concept of change in terms of our national institutions, symbols and our Constitution.
Let me say to the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) that I found it rather interesting that he talked about the rules of this House and that it said so much for the rules of this House that a member of the opposition had talked out previous bills. 1 think if the hon. member looked at this record honestly he probably would find he is the record holder in this House for talking out private members' bills, and I question whether he was being very sincere when he said the bill had been talked out and derided the very rules he has used so adequately and so well in the past. Maybe he applies this only to his own bills and not to other private members' bills.
What is before us today is how we preserve from the past which is best, and how we also prepare plans and take steps to create in Canada the symbols needed for the future? Is there a happy middle ground for those two views? I am sure all members of this House would agree that our symbols are to be those that best reflect the Canada of today. In order to best reflect the Canada of today those symbols and words must also have a bearing on the past. In other words, a symbol cannot stand in isolation in an immediate time-frame; a symbol must also have its sustenance in, and have been built on, the foundation of the past.
What worries me about this bill is not necessarily what it purports to do but the manner in which it purports to do it. That is, if you are not for the bill somehow you might be against Canada, you are against change or you do not want national institutions changed. At least as I view the bill, that is not the question that is before us, but rather how do we best preserve that which has been and build for the future. That is the issue. It is for that reason I believe, with all respect to the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) that his motivation for the bill is wrong. I have no question about his sincerity in wanting to change Dominion Day to Canada Day.
You don't understand the bill.

Just a minute. Let me finish and I will read it to you. If you have a few minutes I will tell you all about it.
The motivation of the Secretary of State is clearly spelled out in both his speech today and the press conference he has given as carried by the Canadian Press. The changes he wants are related to this statement: "We are no longer a colony of the British empire". That is the motivation. In other words, anything that might smack of the past, by natural extension, is colonial. Therefore everything we change in this House is valid, new and relevant. I reject that kind of thinking.
I do not believe that because something has been preserved over many years it is, first of all, obsolete. Second, I do not believe that people can look to the future without looking back as well. In Roman times there was a two-headed, two-faced figure.
A Conservative.

He might have been a Conservative, and if he was I give him credit because he was successful. The point of the symbol was this. He both looked to the past and to the future, which indicates there can be no future without having looked to the past. That is the issue I want to relate to today.
When one looks at the Canada of 1864, and even before then-
