If you want to speak and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the House leader give you time, you should rise on your feet. I am sure it would be a new experience for you.
Canada in that period of time had many small isolated communities clinging basically to the 49th parallel. In addition, it was a country made up of people who had vision for the future and wanted to create the country on the basis of the experience they had either in the old countries or in this country. That is the kind of people they were.
The word "dominion" in itself is not a word that should be denigrated in this House. It should not have any demeaning connotations put to it such as I have heard today. It should not be regarded as colonial. I do not understand why members would feel that word is negative. Most of us who obtained our education in this country were given a very special sense of pride. When we saw a map of Canada with the countries around it shown in various colours, the one colour Canada generally had was red and across it was printed "The Dominion of Canada".
Liberal red.

It might have been Liberal red, if that makes you feel better. What made me feel good was that it was a Dominion of Canada that belonged to all of us. Having said that, I do not know why that attitude should necessarily be thrown in the ash can today.
The Canada of that period was a Canada under attack. In the United States the argument of manifest destiny was very strong. It was an attitude that saw the United States expand its territory to the Pacific, both through war and through land acquisition.
In 1858, twelve years before Manitoba, with a population of
11,000,	became known as the postage stamp province, a resolution was passed in the Minnesota state legislature indicating a desire by the legislators of that period to annex Red River. There were other places in this country which went through that same type of turmoil during that period of time.

With respect to the name chosen for our country, if we read the journals of that period we find there was much debate on what the name should be. Should it just be "Canada"? Should it be the "Kingdom of Canada"? The resolution finally proposed the "Dominion of Canada".
It has already been stated here that Psalm 72:8 was the basis. I want to dwell on that for a minute because not only is it found in Psalm 72:8 but the ancient prophet Zechariah also spoke of the same words and uttered the same words. The name had a very religious meaning to the people of that period of time. It was felt that He, not the Prime Minister of Canada and not even the Monarch in the same sense, was to be supreme and sovereign. He should have dominion from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. No matter how much people want to denigrate that, that remains part of our history.
I for one do not believe we as people or as legislators do service to the present generation or future generations by hanging crepe over the word and saying it does not apply or that it is colonial and that therefore we must end its use. I do not think we serve ourselves or future generations by doing that.
The sovereignty which is inherent in those verses was important not only for religious reasons but also for political reasons. I want to deal with that for just a minute. I say openly that I am indebted to Senator Eugene Forsey for much of the material to which I am going to refer. My House leader also referred to it. I will not quote it, but I believe Senator Forsey-some 25 years ago, in fact-put forward some very cogent arguments as to why Dominion Day had meaning. First, I believe the words "Dominion Day" had a religious connotation; and if we are people who believe that faith does not change and principles do not change, then that principle still remains today and is still valid today. That is the first point.
Second, the material pointed out to everyone that the Fathers of Confederation felt that Canada had a manifest destiny. While we might have gone about it in a way different from that of our American friends to the south, we also had a manifest destiny, and that manifest destiny was also to create a dominion. From how far to how far? From sea to sea. We did it through means other than those used by our American friends. We allowed provinces in. My own province comes to mind. Because of its area and economic base one might have said it was not yet qualified to become a province in 1870. However it was allowed in. Why? Because the Fathers of Confederation knew that if the manifest of the Canadian people was to be realized, they would have to bring in these colonies and make them feel part of the dominion.
I say with a great amount of pride that I believe that the concept of dominion from sea to sea went even further in the time of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, not because he was a member of the party I support but because I think Canadians generally recognized that he developed that concept one step further. He developed it to the northern sea. We were a

There was another reason why the word was chosen. The Fathers of Confederation wanted a constitutional form of government similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom. Perhaps it is here that I have the greatest difficulty with the argument of the Secretary of State. The reason I have difficulty with his argument is not because of his sincere desire to want to change the word and because he feels that "Canada Day" better reflects Canada today. What it seems to be based on is that the principles we inherited from the United Kingdom somehow have not served us well. I say they have served us well.
Some hon. Members; Hear, hear!

If we believe this country is bilingual and therefore say that that is valid to preserve, and if we go further and say that this country is multicultural and therefore it is valid to preserve those cultures, then why is it suddenly not valid to preserve a basic culture which has been so influential not just in this country but right around the world? If one takes a look at a constitution which is to be similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom, where better can we reflect it than in this Parliament or in the parliamentary system? Surely all members of this House, regardless of what background they come from, will argue with every breath they have that this is the best system under which we can serve the people who elect us. Surely there are defenders of the parliamentary system in this House who will argue that this is the best system.
Oh, yes, there might be a need for change, and I have a few changes in mind myself.

There was another reason that the word "dominion" had importance for the Fathers of Confederation. Over this last year we have been arguing in the constitutional committee, in this House and across the country about the balance between the powers needed by a federal, national, central government and the powers of a province or the provinces. In the United States an argument developed for a long period of time over the so-called concept of states' rights, namely, that the individual states had exclusive powers and that they would simply devolve certain powers to the central government for the benefit of the entire nation.
The word "dominion" in Canada had another concept. The Fathers of Confederation wanted a strong national government. Residual powers would remain with the federal government, and I have always been a believer in that. The Fathers of Confederation understood and knew that if the federal

government did not have certain powers, that string of colonies hugging the 49th parallel not only would be faced with threats from the south but also would not have the cohesion needed to develop a country stretching from sea to sea.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, just to set the record straight, I take notice of the remarks of the hon. member and reserve the right of the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) to raise a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, in starting my comments I, too, should like to pay tribute to Terry Fox. Earlier today the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) expressed how all Canadians feel about his accomplishments and contribution to our country. The only Fitting tribute, as was indicated in several newspaper editorials, that Canadians could render to him would be to double our efforts in an attempt to find a solution to the terrible disease which cost him his life.
The bill before us seeks to replace the name "Dominion Day" with the words "Canada Day".

In French, today's bill would substitute the words "fete du Canada" for "fete du Dominion".

It is with great pleasure that I take this opportunity to suggest why the proposed change in the name of our national holiday is not only fitting but also profoundly significant.
I should like to stress three points in my comments. First, the word "dominion" has an ambiguous meaning, both legally and even in dictionaries.

Second, since the word "dominion" has no French equivalent, the act overlooks or ignores one third of Canada's population.

Third, I stress the necessity to have symbols, holidays and institutions in Canada to which all Canadians can relate.
I should like to turn to the matter of the ambiguous meaning. The word "dominion" has a time-honoured place in our nation's history, dating from the birth of confederation. The hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) and other speakers referred to this today. The name was suggested, as we are told in the history books, by Sir Leonard Tilley as an alternative to "kingdom" and was taken from the Seventy-second Psalm:
He shall have dominion also from sea to sea-
This line will always have special significance for Canadians. The phrase "from sea to sea" conveys perhaps better than any other the pride we feel in our vast land, yet the word "dominion" has an ambiguous meaning. In 1921, Prime Minister Lloyd George asked the British House of Commons:
What does Dominion Status mean?
He was speaking on a motion that the House approve the articles of agreement for a treaty between Great Britain and Ireland signed on December 6, 1921, in the opening words of which the following was stated:
Ireland shall have the same constitutional status in the Community of Nations known as the British Empire as the Dominion of Canada, the Commonwealth of Australia, the Dominion of New Zealand, and the Union of South Africa.
Mr. Lloyd George said that it was difficult and dangerous to give a definition. Indeed, he explained that at an imperial conference held earlier in the year all the dominion delegates had been anxious to avoid a rigid definition.
I see the hon. House leader of the official opposition is returning to his seat. I hope he pays some attention to my remarks because I think some of my points have significance.

speechtext: Lloyd George knew my father.

As I was saying, Lloyd George indicated in the British House of Commons in 1921 that it was difficult and dangerous to give a definition to the words "dominion status". Also he explained that at an imperial conference held earlier in the year all the dominion delegates had been anxious to avoid a rigid definition. They had felt that to define precisely was "not the way of the British Constitution". Mr. Lloyd George continued:
Many of the Premiers delivered notable speeches in the course of that Conference, emphasizing the importance of not defining too precisely what the relations of the Dominions were with ourselves, what were their powers, and what was the limit of the power of the Crown. It is something that has never been defined by an Act of Parliament, even in this country, and yet it works perfectly.
I suggest to the House leader of the official opposition that this is fine for constitutional lawyers, but a country such as Canada needs something which is more precise and has more meaning for its national holiday.
These quotations were taken from a book by K. C. Wheare, "The Statute of Westminster and Dominion Status", published in 1942. I do not intend to get into a long discourse on the meaning of "dominion status". Suffice it to say it was the term used to describe the constitutional position of the territo-

rial communities known as the Dominion of Canada, the Commonwealth of Australia, the Dominion of New Zealand, the Union of South Africa, the Irish Free State and Newfoundland. In his book Wheare attempts to define dominion status and the significance of the Statute of Westminster in that definition. However, in the final paragraph of his 303 page study he wrote:
It is doubtful whether the Statute has succeeded completely in the first of the tasks which, in the words of the King's Speech in 1931, it was intended to perform-"to make clear the powers of Dominion Parliaments".
That question is very much an unsettled one today.
The House leader of the opposition said that on July 1 we celebrate a concept. I take issue with that. Yes, dominion status is a concept. The extent to which the federal and provincial governments have powers in relation to the mother parliament is a concept. But Canadians need more than that when it comes to our national holiday. We need more than a concept; we need something about which we can all be proud. I suggest to the hon. member that it is hard for Canadians who are not so familiar with our constitutional past to feel pride in a concept, to get their teeth into it and to get their minds and souls into a concept.
Some references were made by the House leader of the opposition and by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) to remarks made by Senator Eugene Forsey. With all due respect, I suggest to those two hon. members that they are out of touch with reality. How many Canadians read Senator Forsey?

There was no provision for any kind of basic instruction in Canadian history. There was no provision for the Government of Canada to have any input whatsoever into the curricula of our schools. However, the sad fact remains that many young Canadians are not steeped in Canadian constitutional history, nor are they steeped in the origins of Canada by any stretch of the imagination. I also mentioned the fact that the word "dominion" has no equivalent in French. According to the Robert dictionary, "Dominion" means domination or power, and I quote:
Each one of the states, now independent, which makes up the British Union and whose foreign policy was inspired by the United Kingdom.

[English)
I suggest to members opposite that any young Canadian who looked into a dictionary and saw this definition, which is in the Le Dictionnaire Robert, which says that Canada does not have control over its external policies, would be gravely misled. Nevertheless, this is the definition in a Canadian dictionary which is in use and which is sold in many provinces today.
That is a French dictionary.

The hon. member opposite says-

-a French dictionary, but the fact remains that that dictionary is used in most schools. Perhaps it will be found on the table before us today. It can be found in most bookstores in Quebec. Indeed, anyone looking up the word "Dominion" in one of those dictionaries to find out its meaning will have absolutely no idea whatsoever of its current meaning with respect to Canada.

That is the problem. The problem is that the word is fine to constitutional lawyers. The word is fine to parliamentarians who have time to reflect on the matter. However, it has no precise meaning for the vast majority of Canadians who do not have the leisure time to reflect upon great matters such as this.
The thrust of my remarks has been directed toward the necessity to have in Canada symbols, holidays and institutions to which all Canadians can relate. Not so long ago I felt that the Canadian lack of national pride was perhaps our greatest redeeming quality. The displays of emotion for flag and country as favoured by our neighbours to the south often seemed excessive to the more reserved Canadians. However, at the present time when our country is marked by division and lack of communication I feel that we need symbols to which all Canadians can relate. This is a point which I do not feel has been adequately considered by members opposite.

Mr. Speaker, I think there is an urgent need to define our country, to provide common symbols, especially in my riding of Laurier, in Montreal East, which spans St. Lawrence Boulevard, where East meets West. The national issue is urgently felt there. We put up a hard fight during the referendum campaign. Maybe that is something members opposite are not aware of, but I can tell you that the Canadian flag played a major role in our referendum victory, as Prof. Gerard Laforest pointed out so well before the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Constitution when he said, and I quote:
Where do you think we would be if during the referendum there had not been a distinctive Canadian flag? Would you have seen those who favoured staying in this country, in Quebec holding up the Red Ensign everywhere?

I think we very deeply need symbols in this country.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I do not feel that the hon. members of the official opposition realize the war that we are waging today, at this very minute, for the hearts and minds of Quebecers. I can refer to an article which appeared in Le Droit last October 28, 1980, in which the newspaper pointed out that Quebecers, more than other Canadians, realized that the first of July was Canada's birthday. However, the study also revealed that Quebecers participated less actively than other Canadians in the celebrations for Canada's birthday. This may [DOT] perhaps be the result, or the natural result, of having another important holiday, la Fete Nationale du Quebec, which precedes it by only one week. We parliamentarians here should look to the one-third of Canadians who are of neither British nor French origin. When I say one-third of Canadians, I feel that the figure is probably a lot greater than that. The hon. Leader of the Official Opposition suggested that the government should wait and that it must satisfy the House that the overwhelming number of Canadians would be satisfied with this change prior to embarking upon it. I would suggest that the hon. members opposite have no concept of leadership, that they have no understanding of the fact that the Parliament of our country should try to set some sort of pace for the nation and not get too far ahead of it, as I think it has been said, but perhaps take a lead to show the way. It is quite obvious that they have no conception whatsoever of the importance of leadership and the importance of showing the way to other Canadians in matters of our national government. They would have us wait until the matter emerged from Canadians by some sort of osmosis. They would wait until people right across the country got up and started walking up and down the streets crying out for such a matter. I would suggest that if governments waited that long to act in any matter, there would be very little activity conducted in the affairs of any nation.
As I said previously, I would suggest to hon. members opposite that they again look to immigrants for the answer. I would like to point out to them a couple of facts. First of all, an element which characterizes my riding, in addition to its dualistic nature, is the fact that every month I receive in my office, a list of at least 100 new citizens. I would like to read out the names of some of them on the most recent list: Mrs. Ourania Voudouris; Miss Sok Than Ang; Mr. Mbang Bousso Hadji Ngarmorio; Mr. Kailesh Hasmukhabhai Gopalbhai and
Mrs. Leontina Maria Varao Macedo. I suppose I should apologize to the people whose names I have read out, because of my pronunciation. I do not know any of these people and it is likely that I did not do great justice to the pronunciation of their names. The point I wanted to stress is that every month in my constituency there are 100 people like the five people whose names I have just read out. Every month across Canada there are probably 10,000 Canadiens who become new citizens and who are looking for Canadian symbols to identify with, and who are unfortunately, not aware and have no way of being aware of the fractured history which has preceded their arrival. For these people, the word "Canada" was and is the magic word.

Canada for them is a magic word. As Naim Kattan so rightly said in "L'Arrivee":
Canada! That was the magic word that stirred in us feelings of expectation and hope as well as of worry and anguish.

I think that this House should recognize these facts and that it should recognize that the greatest thing we have in common amongst us as Canadians is Canada. It is an international word. It is a word which is recognized all over the world, in all countries and in all languages. I would suggest that it is a word which is entirely appropriate to our national day.
Hear, hear!
This July 1 let us really celebrate Canada Day!
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I too want to rise in my place today and speak both in favour of Canada and against Canada Day. We have had some interesting presentations here this afternoon. We have heard from the minister himself. I was disappointed to think that a minister of the Crown, the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) who is in charge of communications, could not give us a better research document than he did on the history of the words "Dominion Day" and on why we should attempt to change it. I thought that we could have had a better explanation from him. His colleague, the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) chose to give us a long litany of the bills which have been brought before the House and have been turned down for one reason or another. He then went on to give us a list of the newspaper headlines, going back many years, in which Canada Day was being proposed. Again, he made no attempt to look into the history of the words "Dominion Day" and why some of us feel the name worth preserving. I thought my colleague, the House leader of my party, took a very fair approach. He looked at this concept of changing the name from Dominion Day to Canada Day and decided that it deserved some discussion by parliamentarians, something we have not had a chance to discuss in that fashion before. The hon. member is proposing that we amend this motion before the House so that the subject matter will go before a committee, with which I certainly agree.
June 29, 1981

I thought the most telling speech that we have heard so far today was given by my colleague, the hon. member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Epp). He gave an incisive analysis of the origins and the meanings of Dominion Day going back to 1867 when our forefathers and those who had reason to do so chose a name for this country. The hon. member for Provencher explained in a very logical way why they chose the words they did. The proof of his logic was shown by the effect he had on government members who intervened as much as they could because they were embarrassed, I would suggest, by some of the arguments which the hon. member for Provencher used.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Berger). I think he made an attempt to go into some of the early meanings of the naming of July 1. He gave his view for the reasons for change.
A piece of paper was passed to me from one of my colleagues opposite a few moments ago. The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) handed me a definition from a French language dictionary. In this dictionary the word "dominion" is described as being an English word. This just goes to show why we have some of the problems we do in our schools. It is obvious that we have a French dictionary which tells us that the word "dominion" is an English word, and yet I can show my hon. colleague that the word is actually a French word, preserved by the English language back in the time of the King James version of the Bible. Prior to that, "dominion" was a French word. However, I will get the appropriate quotation for my colleague. It is interesting to hear the different views one can get on issues like this.
As we all know, Dominion Day is the correct, legal and official designation of July 1, as three acts of Parliament have already determined in the past. Today, with Bill C-37 and the amendment before us, we are asked to formally change the name from Dominion Day to Canada Day. Yet it is worth noting that the government has for some years now been using the appellation Canada Day and not Dominion Day in its press releases and commercials in advertising our national holiday. In short, the government has deliberately been breaking the law of the land by unilaterally, and without debate, changing the name of Canada's birthday from Dominion Day to Canada Day. There is no moral or ethical excuse for the government breaking the law of the land.
The name of former senator Eugene Forsey has been mentioned several times today. I think it is appropriate that he has been mentioned because he is the one person who has given some serious thought to the meaning of the words "Dominion Day". As most of us know here, he was a former research director for the Canadian Labour Congress. He was also a former Liberal senator. He is one of the foremost authorities on Canadian constitutional law, in spite of what my colleague from Laurier has said. Former senator Forsey, said:
-parliamentary responsible government rests on the rule of law. The government must not break the law, anymore than the ordinary person,-or rules of Parliament, anymore than your ordinary member. Majorities are not enough: they must be majorities acting within the law, within the rules.
Holidays Act
There is no denying that "Canada Day" has crept into popular usage in this country, and it is often used interchangeably with "Dominion Day", but what we are being asked to do with Bill C-37 is to make the formal change and discard a uniquely Canadian term Dominion Day forever and ever. I say this is a mistake and I have yet to see or hear a compelling or convincing argument for this change.
Bill C-37 is to erase Dominion Day from the books. In short, it attempts to turn our backs on our history, cast away our beginnings, our heritage, our tradition. Some would say that we are starting anew but, in my mind, you cannot have progress without continuity, nor continuity without progress.
A well known Canadian historian, Michael Bliss, has said:
Canadians are a people who remember their present and think it's their history.
Certainly, this is true of this government. On December 21, 1976, the then secretary of state introduced a bill into the House of Commons. It proposed, among other things, to change the name of Dominion Day to Canada Day, and Victoria Day to Queen's birthday. Victoria Day was not a holiday to celebrate any Queen's birthday; it was a holiday decreed to celebrate the birthday of a particular queen, one queen, Queen Victoria, and it is only meaningful to Canadians as Victoria Day. I bring this to the House's attention because there is and has been an assault by Liberal governments on tradition in Canada. But the moment that traditions are discarded and our heritage is ignored, the government does the society irreparable damage. I am one who believes that society is a partnership not only among those who are living but among those who are dead, and those who are to be born. Within society, there is a tremendous store of wisdom, a treasury to which it is the duty of each generation to make its characteristic contribution. By discarding traditions, one loses one's roots. Any change of the name of Dominion Day is not insignificant, since by changing a name which is rich in meaning one also changes the meaning of our national holiday. I would favour, perhaps, a "Canada Day" but not as a substitute for "Dominion Day". July 1 is celebrated because it is our birthday and only the term Dominion Day addresses this fact.
I believe in what Professor Kenneth McNaught said in the following words:
No person can be healthy if he does not know where he comes from and why he did what he did. Thus we should recall that Dominion Day was decreed to celebrate a very Canadian event and some fundamental Canadian decisions.
The minute we sever our links with the past, we lose the sense of ourselves, our country. We fall prey to building transitory and fragile sand castles which are washed away by the tides of fashion and arbitrary change, due of course to arbitrary reason. We would thus drift like tumbleweed blown to and fro, having lost our worth, or reason to be, our very life.
Why then would anyone wish a change? Well, I can think of two reasons. Either those advocates of a change are ashamed of our past and the use of the word "dominion" as it applies to our country since, of course, at its birth, our country was known as Dominion of Canada; or one may argue that the

term Dominion Day no longer applies to our national holiday, July 1.
I would ask if anyone is ashamed of the appellation "dominion". I would hope not. If so, I would venture to say that it would be because those people betray a lack of knowledge about Canada's historic beginnings. For some reason, and I have read the arguments, some believe that the term Dominion of Canada and hence Dominion Day is outdated, that it is tainted with the brush of colonialism. However, I would submit that a true reading of our beginnings and an understanding of Canada at its inception might lead members to conclude otherwise.
What then did the title Dominion of Canada mean to Canadians on July 1, 1867, at confederation? I turn to the front page of The Globe and Mail of that date. It reads:
We celebrate then today an event of much greater importance than the confederation merely of three or four provinces-the union of the maritime provinces with Canada. We celebrate the inauguration of a new nationality; to which are committed the interests of Christianity and civilization over a territory larger than that of the ancient Roman empire, larger, too, than the territory which is controlled by the great neighbouring republic, and with a population greater than that with which the United States began their career ninety years ago. In the duties, therefore, of the present, and in the hope and aspirations which gild our future, there is room and scope ample enough for the purest patriotism and the loftiest ambition. Let us hope that Canadians-using the word in its new and large acceptation-will worthily fulfil the duties which Providence has confided to them.
For the Fathers of Confederation and the people at the time of confederation, the term dominion did not suggest subservience, as it has been suggested a number of times by government members, nor was it British. It was distinctively Canadian, chosen by a father of confederation, Sir Leonard Tilley, from the seventy-second psalm, which reads:
He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.
What more aptly describes Canada, which extends from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean, than does dominion? Or, as the motto on our coat of arms says, a mari usque ad mare-from sea to sea.
This word dominion declared the destiny of Canada to rule from sea to sea and from the St. Lawrence River to the north pole. It is a term as rich and as meaningful today as it was then. I would submit that it was an inspired choice.
Confederation was a positive decision to create a union, monarchical in principle, parliamentary in form and traditional in spirit, a union based on peace, order and good government, which was decidedly and deliberately different from the United States. It was a supreme act of faith, defying economics, American manifest destiny and, some would say, geography. We stamped our nationhood on the northern half of the continent, calling our country the dominion of Canada.
One need only read the writings of the period to be struck by the enthusiasm for this new country which fired the imagination. The term dominion connoted an expanse of territory matched only by the scope of opportunity in this new land. It was a time for gladness, celebration, in anticipation of a
bright, noteworthy future. Laurier gave voice to this optimism later when he said, "The twentieth century belongs to Canada", speaking to the Canadian Club of Ottawa in 1904. I stress again that dominion was a made-in-Canada term and in no way did it suggest subservience or a lesser status for Canada. There is no need to be ashamed of the word dominion. Far from it.
There are others I have come across who assert that for French-speaking Canadians the word "dominion" is a verbal oddity which serves to inflame old colonial wounds, that somehow the word dominion offends Quebec. It was argued before the referendum that it was time to change Dominion Day to Canada Day and now we are told that perhaps with the coming of a new Constitution it is time now to make the change. Acknowledging that in 1867 there were basically two founding cultures, to which many others have since been added, we find that the word "dominion" is not an Anglo-Saxon word. It is actually an old French word, it had dropped out of use but was preserved in the English Bible and the English Book of Common Prayer.
The French translation of dominion is "puissance" meaning power, or "souverainete", meaning sovereignty, which the new nation Canada would have. One just has to ask the question, how can a prime minister of French and English descent, who pretends to be worried about national unity, really be serious or be believed when he is prepared to forget or ignore the historic significance of the word "dominion" as applied to our national holiday on July 1?
The word dominion, coming from the Bible, emphasizes the religious basis of the new nation. As well, it asserts lordship, the primacy of the new nation over its parts wherein Canada was to be one dominion divided into four provinces. Moreover, dominion was intended to assert Canada's adherence to the monarchy. Indeed, the first choice of the fathers was to call the new country the kingdom of Canada.
Finally, I have heard murmurings that Dominion Day is offensive to new Canadians and thus perhaps, to make them feel more at home the name should be changed to Canada Day. The hon. member for Laurier stressed this point. It puzzles me when I try to understand why a person would want to emigrate to this country knowing that our national holiday is Dominion Day and then feel betrayed on arriving here to find that the name is not Canada Day. To use that kind of argument on behalf of new Canadians astonishes me, but we hear it fairly often.
The hon. member who spoke second for the government today is not a native-born Canadian. He is a native of the United Kingdom. The hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), who is my Ottawa member and who is interjecting the most, is not a Canadian by birth either. I would be the last to take away the right for them to speak that way, but to think that those two members feel that strongly about the name of the country surprises me.
Immigrants come to Canada, I am sure, because they like our country, what it stands for, and our way of life. In Canada, we encourage multiculturalism and unity within diversity. We
June 29, 1981

see an excellent example of this fact in the annual Caravan Festival in Toronto. Most new Canadians retain their cultural links and roots and traditions and realize the value of these links. Surely this group of Canadians would be the last to encourage Canada to sever its links with the past, to turn its back on its heritage. I do not believe it. Moreover, as new Canadians, they knew of Canada's heritage and tradition and way of life before they chose to come here.
If there is no reason to be ashamed of the title "Dominion", why then make the change to Canada Day? Is it because dominion no longer applies? How can that be?
Why is July 1 the date of our national holiday? Quite simply, and I think we are all in agreement, it is because July 1 is Canada's birthday. We celebrate confederation on July 1 and surely it strains one's imagination to imply that Dominion Day is no longer apt. It remains historically and geographically meaningful.
Returning to the front page of the Globe on July 1, 1867, we read the following:
Stamped with a familiar name, which in the past has borne a record sufficiently honourable to entitle it to be perpetuated with a more comprehensive import, the DOMINION OF CANADA, on this First day of July, in the year of grace, eighteen hundred and sixty-seven, enters on a new career of national existence.
Confederation was a union of Canadas, that is, Ontario and Quebec, formerly Upper Canada and Canada West and Lower Canada and Canada East respectively, with New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The provinces joined to form, not Canada, but a new country, a larger Dominion of Canada. The Fathers of Confederation chose the term "dominion". They would not have agreed to calling July 1 Canada Day.
It is natural and only makes sense if we call July 1 Dominion Day if, of course, we refer to Canada's birthday. It is not possible to speak with accuracy of a 114th birthday without posing any question about ancestors who called themselves Canadians before confederation, whereas Dominion Day means only one thing: Canada's birthday, July 1.
Surely the point of having a national holiday at all is to celebrate our country, its history past and present. Canada Day would change the meaning of our national holiday. The term Canada Day is alien to confederation, a time when Canadians spoke of the grandiose Dominion of Canada. One of the great failings of Canadians is that many do not have a strong sense of our history and surely the purpose of a national holiday is to sit back and reflect and appreciate our history and where we have come from. Yet now we are asked to cast our history aside and to banish the name Dominion Day forever.
The proposal to change the formal appellation of Dominion Day to Canada Day unfortunately is not an isolated incident or issue but is becoming increasingly characteristic of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who places abstract reasoning above prescription and tradition, though we all know he has a well-developed concern for the judgment of history in relation to himself. We are witnessing arrogance. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the government stand on the Constitution,
Holidays Act
nor in the famous, or should I say infamous, interview on New Year's Eve with the Prime Minister when he said essentially that if the country were to break up because of what his government was trying to do-

Mr. Speaker, prior to our recessing at the supper hour I was making some comments about the fact that there are certain traditions in this country which I feel at times are being lost. I was discussing the use of the words "Dominion Day" to designate our national holiday as being one of those traditions. I was comparing it to some changes to the Constitution we have been faced with and suggested this was a parallel situation. The Secretary of State took exception to that on a point of order.
Be that as it may, I would like to proceed with the thought in mind that Canada Day itself as a term is not rooted in any kind of tradition. It is abstract and means very little to most Canadians. However, we could institute a new holiday, a new national holiday choosing to call it Canada Day rather than heritage day as has been proposed in the past. Dominion Day, on the other hand, is rich in meaning to many Canadians. It is correct and it is entirely appropriate as well.
The hon. member for Vaudreuil when speaking this afternoon made reference to the fact that it was passing strange to

June 29, 1981

him that we were not in a position to call our national holiday Canada Day. I noticed in researching this presentation that back on May 6, 1980, as reported at page 764 of Hansard, he said almost exactly the same as he said today, namely:
We want to celebrate our national holiday using the name of our country, as every other country would surely want to do.
The strange thing is that there are only three other countries in the world that do that now. It was mentioned earlier today that Australia and New Zealand do that, and the third country is Pakistan. It is not factual that most countries call their national holidays by the name of the country. Only three countries out of many have chosen to do that.
Let us look at what has been done in other countries in addition to the fact that only three call their national holidays by their country name. The United States does not call their national holiday, Independence Day, by its name. We have not heard an explanation as to why they would not want to do that. Nor does France call its national holiday, Bastille Day, France day. I do not know why they do not want to change Bastille Bay to France Day, but there is probably a good reason. Why does Quebec, for instance, not change St. Jean Baptiste Day to Quebec day if that sort of move has a lot of meaning to people?
In conclusion I should like to quote the following from the Ottawa Journal of June 30, 1979:
Dominion Day has at least a ring of sorts to it. Whereas Canada Day does sound as though it were put together in a hurry when there wasn't time to think of anything better.
That is the way it has been done this time too, I would suggest. Parenthetically, one would think we had no economic problems that are more important for consideration today than this business of Canada Day. The article went on to read:
Perhaps the greatest danger with Canada Day is that somehow it might get twisted into "Day Canada" along with those other horrors; Supply Canada, Manpower Canada, Environment Canada, etc.
I would conclude by saying: Canada week, yes, but Canada Day, never.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been so much criticism of the government in the past, sometimes accurate and sometimes perceived, but mostly perceived by the opposition, that I was surprised today to witness a debate on whether we should call July 1 Canada Day. I expected to come into the House and see members of the opposition rise to their feet and cheer. Much to my surprise I came here and found the same type of leadership of members opposite that made them oppose the flag and the Constitution, and now makes them oppose Canada Day.
During the last several speeches there has been quite some reference to history. Let me quote Harry S. Truman, a former President of the United States, who said:
Men make history and not the other way 'round. In periods where there is no leadership, society stands still. Progress occurs when courageous, skilful leaders seize the opportunity to change things for the better.
For some strange reason, the Tories are the captives of history: if it happened in the past it is good. The lesson that men make history but history does not make men is one that the Tories have not learned and will never learn. Perhaps this is a period of no leadership, as Harry S. Truman suggested, and things will look up in the future.
I witness opposition for the sake of opposition here. I think there has to be some proposing as well as opposing. I am surprised the opposition did not grasp this opportunity to present this matter as a private member's bill, to which the government would have responded in the affirmative.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) alluded to the fact that three previous speakers from the government side were not born in Canada. To ease his mind let me tell him that I was born in Canada, my mother was born in Canada and my father was born in Canada. However, my maternal grandfather was born in Ireland, a Protestant Irishman. My paternal grandparents were born in Italy. They did not come to Canada because July 1 was called Dominion Day; they came to Canada for jobs. My grandmother came here when she was 16 and lived to be 94. At least once a year she would say how lucky we were to be living in Canada. On July 1, if you had told her we were celebrating Dominion Day, she would not have known what you were talking about. However, if you had told her that on Canada Day we were celebrating the importance of living in Canada, she would have rejoiced.
Why is it so important in our country to have these symbols? I have travelled across this land and I know that our very strength is our greatest weakness. In Newfoundland they are still talking about 1949, and there is a strong Irish element. In Nova Scotia the strength of Cape Breton is in its Scottish ancestry. In Quebec they go back 300 years in French and Quebec culture. The Acadians do not even consider themselves Quebecois; they consider themselves maritimers. Ontario is multicultured. In the west there are Germans, Ukrainians and there is western separatism. Superimposed on all this are 20 or 30 additional cultures in our country.
We in the Liberal party have traditionally tried to tie this country to a core. In the heat of the declaration of war, Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie King said the following in New York on June 17, 1941:
Our declaration was signed by the King upon the recommendation of His Majesty's Canadian ministers. The King's Proclamation was in the name of Canada.
Traditionally the Liberals have built up our nation and our sense of nation. At the same time, as evidenced by our willingness to support the Commonwealth and other countries of the Commonwealth, we understand its historic significance.
I fully appreciate the richness of our English past and the meaning of "dominion". It is in our courts and in our parliaments. It is a product of that history. However, we need not only recall our history. Let us also remember the symbols of our nation, and the name Canada on Canada Day is that symbol.

The hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) talked about the history of several bills proposing the name Canada Day. I was not only shocked but dismayed to find as a new member that we have been trying for so long to change the name to Canada Day. The hon. member talked about media support. He spoke about group support. He spoke about public support. If we were to place before any municipal council in this country the choice between Dominion Day and Canada Day for July 1, in at least 90 per cent of the cases these grassroots town councils would say, "We want Canada Day". The Tories oppose this.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) asks whether this is the right time. There is a story about the right time. When Abraham Lincoln was about to sign the emancipation proclamation, his hand was shaking. His clerk said to him, "Why is your hand shaking, Mr. President?" Mr. Lincoln said, "I want to rest. I have shaken at least a thousand hands this day, and I do not want my signature to be weak. I do not want history to say I hesitated". That is the history of the party opposite. Hon. members opposite are waiting for the right time. Was there a right time for the flag? Was there a right time for the Constitution? Is there a right time to call July 1 Canada Day?
Between six o'clock and eight o'clock today I asked a person standing in front of the chamber, "What do you call July 1?" He said, "Canada Day". The public knows this, the NDP knows this, the government knows this, the gallery knows this-but the Tories are waiting for the right time. The Tories are waiting for history to catch up with them.
The hon. member for Provencher says Canadians are divided, that this is not the right time and that the government has divided Canadians. How did we divide Canadians? We proposed a charter which gave Canadians a certain dignity which governments cannot take away. We suggested they are no longer colonials and that we should have our own Constitution. We suggested a formula to which everyone agreed in 1971. That is what is supposedly dividing Canada. I suggest to the opposition that what is dividing Canada is the fact that the opposition lost the last election, proved that it could not make inroads in the east and is living off western division. I have said this before and I will say it again: if there is division in this country, it is because the Tories have fostered that division.
It is because of Trudeau, nobody else.

Can we not begin to plan so that the reality in Ottawa now can be the reality across Canada?
Yesterday I made a phone call, Mr. Speaker, to invite someone from Ottawa to come to Waterloo for a holiday. This young woman said: I cannot leave Ottawa until after the July 1 celebration. There is a sense of celebration here in the capital, and I wish it were so across the country. I want to suggest to the government that before we change the name, we should involve the people who are going to help us celebrate. In my experience those people have been the new Canadians, people who are now part of the multicultural composition of Canada in which we take a great deal of pride.
The minister spoke of July 1 as being representative of the pride we have in Canada and of the hope we have in the future. I concur in those aspirations but I contend they are not yet a reality. The changing of the name without using the process of involving the people in the change is not helpful at this time. Therefore, I am prepared to support our House leader's amendment that we take the next year and invite representatives of the multicultural groups and others across Canada to share with us their recommendations for the name and whether it should be Confederation Day, Dominion of Canada Day, Canada Day, or whatever we agree on. I am prepared to vote for that because I think the importance of meaningful symbols, as we have spoken of them, cannot be underestimated.
Some years ago, Mr. Speaker, in this House the first Canadian governor general, the Right Hon. Vincent Massey, had these words about Canada:
I believe in Canada, with pride in her past, belief in her present, and faith in her future.
I believe in the quality of Canadian life, and in the character of Canadian institutions.
I believe in the Commonwealth of Nations, within whose bounds we have found freedom, and outside which our national life would lose its independent being.
I believe that Canada is one, and that if our minds dwell on those things which its parts have in common, we can find the unity of the whole.
1 believe that with sound work, the spirit of a team, and an awareness of ourselves, we can look forward to achievements beyond our imagining.
I believe what Vincent Massey was saying many decades ago about Canada is what the government and all members of this House wish for Canada: A team spirit, not a country divided. On this day, when there have been so many fitting comments made about the significance of Terry Fox for Canada, I think it is important to recognize that it was not the name Terry Fox that gave reality, it was the substance of what he did and what he stood for. He had a commitment to the betterment of this nation and to drawing Canadians together.
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), in response to the minister, said that government advertising of Canada Day in a sense gets in the way of public acceptance. He went on to speak about what happens when government becomes the propagandist. He spoke about the symbols of national unity, how they should come from the people, and that we should be using here the evolutionary principle. He mentioned the experience of a number of countries in this area. I want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that in offering my observations to the government about timing and direction, I speak with some experience, having been involved in directing the Canadian centennial and mobilizing the spirit there. I speak with some experience as the executive director of the Manitoba centennial, drawing Canadians of that province, indeed all Canadians to celebrate with them. I speak with the experience of a consultant to the government of Prince Edward Island on their centennial. The success of our Canadian centennial and the provincial centennials was not in the fact we proclaimed a day of celebration or a day of special meaning. On July 1, this national day, our area is as proud as are all Canadians to state that we stand on guard for Canada. When we hear so often lately that Canada is facing a struggle between its regions, we should remember that when our forefathers left their various homes it was to come to Canada. They

did not come to one town. They did not come to one province. They left for Canada. In recent overseas consultation and during the five years I lived in West Africa, I have repeatedly sensed how desirable Canada is to people from around the world.

What I am trying to suggest is that in my riding it is not any one group which I can singly represent but there is a multicultural reality. In my riding there are people of German background and there is a Mennonite group. All of the different groups in my riding have a varying degree of suspicion about government motivation.
As I have tried to suggest to the minister before, I am sympathetic. I have been working as a civil servant for the government on behalf of Canada in national celebrations. I understand something about community motivation. For the minister to suggest that somehow these topics are not related to the direction in which government is headed is, it seems to me, a disservice to the motivation which we want, that Canadians identify with it, not as a government initiative but as a Canadian initiative.

deserves addressing, since the argument has been put forward a number of times that what we are trying to do through our amendment is avoid the bitterness which came about as a result of the flag debate. When I was an alderman in the city of Waterloo I served as chairman of community services. It was my responsibility to organize a special observance for Canada week. We drew together some 5,000 young people from kindergarten to grade eight in the Seagram's stadium. We were able to rehearse in song and in word the history of Canada. The matters which have come out of the constitutional discussion and the times when we are most deeply divided are the times when we stop listening to each other. I suggest that there are instruments across this country which can clothe the government's proposals with meaning. The proposal put forward by this party is not an obstructive one, nor is it un-Canadian. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Sports); Liberal Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
I thank your Honour for recognizing me and giving me a chance to speak in this debate. In answer to some of the points that the member of Parliament for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) raised I would point out that this is not exactly what one would call a precipitous debate to change the name of Dominion Day to Canada Day. I can recall that on November 30, 1978, a similar motion was raised by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) who also proposed that this matter be sent to committee. I would point out to the hon. member for Waterloo that his suggestion of sending this bill to a committee for study is exactly what we are trying to do. After all, we are on the second reading of this bill. If we bring this to a vote, if the opposition will permit it to come to a vote, I would suggest that we could very well send it to committee, and these studies he is talking about could very well take place.
As to the point that changing the name from Dominion Day to Canada Day is some kind of propaganda, how can we possibly think that the word "Canada" is propagandist? My God, it is the name of our country. Since when, if we give the name of our country to any day or any act, does that become propaganda? Are we not all, all of us, Canadians in this House? Are we not all Canadians first?
Some time ago I had occasion to represent in Japan the minister of fitness and amateur sport. I would simply point out that, notwithstanding the fact that our nation is made up of many cultures, when those athletes were outside the country they were Canadians, very simply, Canadians; no more, but surely no less.
The hon. member from Quebec made reference a little earlier to the flag, and he raised the question as to whether we would have the flag today, whether we would indeed be blessed with the flag we have now or would we have the flag that we had some time ago. I would suggest to all hon. members that however acrimonious and bitter the debate was at the time, surely the flag is one of the symbols which unites us today. Surely there is not a Canadian who travels anywhere within Canada or outside of Canada who does not have that feeling of pride when he sees his own flag, our very own. It took us 98 years to finally get that most elementary symbol to all sovereign countries.
I think sport does unite us. Because of this, when our athletes travel abroad, they are simply known as Canadians. It does not matter from which ethnic background they come. They perform for us, for a nation as a whole. I do not in any way downgrade or take away from any cultural group here in Canada; but by the same token, it should be said that all of these people, if they chose Canada first, if they came from another country, they chose us. They chose this blessed land. They want to be known first and foremost as Canadians. No one ever said that they would be deprived of their culture. No one ever said that they had to give up their particular language or customs. On the contrary, we believe that because of this diversity, we are stronger, and not only stronger but surely we are more colourful as a nation in the sense that we can share

June 29, 1981
Holidays Act
our differences with one another. In that sense, we are very much richer.
Perhaps the House would be interested to know that notwithstanding the great loss we have felt in the last few days, having lost, I would say, not only one of our foremost athletes, in the sense that he had the great heart of an athlete, but probably one of our foremost heroes since we have become a nation, there are other young people who are in the mold of Terry Fox. This noon hour I took part in a ceremony in honour of a young chap called Steve Maaslain, a cyclist. He left here to bicycle all across the North American continent. I know that when he went from place to place, what he took with him was the symbol of our country. Wherever he went, he was known as a Canadian. He came home to celebrate with us what most of us now call Canada Day and what we would like to call officially Canada Day.
We are in the process of going through these growing pains, but for how long? How long must we go through these growing pains before we can become what we really are? For those of us who have no other culture, as it were, who come from no other country, for people like myself, who were born and raised here in Canada, who went to school here, live here and, God willing, will die in this country, our country is Canada. This is the beginning and the end for us. This is ours. We do not come from England or France or Hungary or Italy. We come from here. The people who come over to this country take on, I guess, the blessings of the country which is here, which is ours, the country where we were born; yet, in spite of all this, cannot call July 1 Canada Day. We cannot bring a bill in this House of Commons so that we can call this celebration what it is. It is our birthday. It is the birthday of this country. It is the birthday of Canadians. I for one am anxiously awaiting the day when once more, or at last, we will have one more symbol to call our own.
Your Honour is aware, as you have heard other hon. members say, that it was not until 1946 that we established Canadian citizenship. Confederation was a supreme act of faith, faith that defied geography, defied economics, defied the "manifest destiny" of the Americans to rule the whole continent from the Rio Grande to the North Pole.
Faith in what? In something beyond economics, beyond the material; faith that the British North American colonies had a heritage worth preserving, worth developing, worth paying an economic price for; faith that on this rock our people could build a great nation, part of a great Commonwealth.
He referred to the "Title of Our Country". He said:
Both choices are enshrined in the word "Dominion" itself, the title which the Fathers gave our country, the title they wrote into the British North America Act, three times over. Where did that title come from, and what does it mean?
The Fathers originally wanted to call the new nation "the Kingdom of Canada." But the Americans raised such a storm that the British government took fright, and insisted on something else. The Fathers for their part, insisted on something that would mark the new and higher status of the federation. Sir Leonard Tilley produced the solution, from the seventy-second psalm: "He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth." His colleagues agreed; the Queen consented; and "Dominion" the new nation became.
That title was "a particularly happy choice" according to Dr. Forsey. He wrote:
The title was a particularly happy one, for more reasons than one. First, and most obviously, it embodied the determination of the Fathers to bring into the Union all the British North American colonies from Newfoundland to British Columbia; "a mari usque ad mare," as our coat-of-arms says. It declared the "manifest destiny" of Canada to rule from the St. Lawrence to the North Pole.
Second, and more important, it emphasized the religious basis of the new nation. Who was to have "dominion"? The King of Israel, the Lord's Anointed: the King, under God.
Third, it proclaimed the basic fact of our two cultures. For "Dominion" is not Anglo-Saxon. It is an old French word which dropped out of use in French but was preserved in our English Bible and our English Book of Common Prayer.
Fourth, it proclaimed, no less unmistakably, our new status. The French translation of "Dominion" is "Puissance," (Power): "Souverainete," (Sovereignty); a far cry indeed from "province" or "colony," a foreshadowing of the independence to come. And it was so recognized at the time. It was meant, Lord Carnarvon told the Queen, just before the Act was passed, "to give greater dignity to the commencement of this great scheme." "Canada", said Edward Blake in 1876, "is not a colony or a province; she is a Dominion, under an Imperial charter which expressly recites that her Constitution is to be similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom."

That served very well Canadians of that time and is still serving Canadians of this time.
1 am a defender of confederation, but 1 know it is because of the multitude, thank God, of other Canadians who came to this land to help it grow and become more universal, that we have this Canada of today. Look at the evolution of Canada from 1867. Look at the significant events that took place since that date. You come to 1933, 1945, and 1949. Then we have the famous flag debate. After that you arrive at something

June 29, 1981
Holidays Act
that I participated in called the Special Joint Committee of the House and Senate on the National Anthem.

In 1965, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Mr. Pearson decided that we would have a national anthem. A committee was set up and we sat on that committee. I am one of the last survivors of that committee still in the House. I sat on that committee with my colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). We agreed that "O Canada" should become our national anthem. Some people were saying: But not now! It is too early! It is premature! Do people know how much time it took us? It was proclaimed in 1980! Frankly, dear colleagues, I think we have been very patient.
Today we are presenting something new, according to certain members. But it is not new. Since 1968, 22 bills on that subject have been introduced by members who are anxious to acknowledge that this holiday, our anniversary, is the anniversary of all Canadians and to call it by its name-Canada Day. Since 1968!
I would probably side, as I do sometimes, with hon. members of the opposition if I thought we are rushing too fast or that it should not take place. I may vote in one way, but sometimes I reflect and say that perhaps we should think a little more. That is not the case in this regard. I would have gone to the Secretary of State and asked, "Why do you not accept the proposed delay?", if he had arrived tonight with a special surprise for the House of Commons to celebrate the 114 years of what we know Canada to be. He is not taking us by surprise. It has been going on and on since 1968. I repeat that we would have had time. We did not see any march or demonstrations in the street, thank God. People know that this matter is being discussed in the House; they could have talked about it. We have not had delegations of people who want to be heard. If we had done what was suggested, if we had had another committee looking at it, there would have never been a Canadian flag.
Is it not time to realize that when we talk about such subject matters, it is fine to be emotional. Canada is an emotional thing for me. It is fine, when we talk about Canada, to quote such people as my dear good friend, Senator Forsey, as was done by my hon. friend from Hamilton. But whom did he keep quoting? I want to be clear. That is why I am speaking more in English than in French tonight. I want to be clearly understood in what I have to say. It has nothing to do with being anti-English or anti-French or a fight between the two. It would be a denial of my entire life if hon. members thought otherwise. Whom did he quote? He quoted lord so-and-so and sir so-and-so. He quoted the Bible. I am a religious person and a believer, but I do not see the relevancy. Is it not anti-Bible to rise and quote the Bible when talking about Canada? Sure, it is in the Bible, but it does not say that because it is a quote from the Bible we cannot follow our inclinations for Canada,
that is, to make it better known and accepted as such. They talked about the United Kingdom and what took place in 1867. They talked about the monarchy. They talked about the dominion. Again they talked about sir so-and-so.
Let us build Canada now for the people of tomorrow irrespective of the people of yesterday. We must respect them, but if we always go back and say, "Yesterday they said that, accordingly we should not move today", I do not know the kind of Canada we would have. If Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir George Etienne Cartier would have had the same kind of attitude, I can tell my good colleagues from British Columbia and everywhere else that we would not be celebrating our one hundred and fourteenth anniversary. But they were people who said it was best for a group of people who lived on a piece of land, which is now called Canada, that we have confederation. Then Mr. Pearson knew that it was best for Canada, knowing that it was divisive and passionate, to have a national anthem. It was best for the future of young Canadians to have a Canadian flag, and soon they will have a Constitution. I agree that we in the country may disagree on the way it is being done. This is debatable, but one matter which is not debatable is the fact that we want a Constitution in Canada, done by Canadians and amended by Canadians. This is a step in the right direction. It is true Canadianization. There is nothing anti-British or anti-monarchy in that. It is just a cold Canadian fact of life.
I should like to call upon my dear colleague, the House leader of the Official Opposition. Perhaps he would like to withdraw his amendment-he knows I am sincere-and accept the fact that we should send the bill to committee. I hope the Secretary of State is listening in case I am making a mistake; I am almost making a proposal for him. I have a few minutes left; I do not want to speak last. Perhaps the hon. member should withdraw his amendment and not send the subject matter to committee after second reading, but send the bill itself. It will not be passed by July 1. Then the point of the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) would be answered, as well as the point of the hon. member from Hamilton who said, "Let's have a committee; let's have this and that." At least we would have second reading tonight and it would be sent to committee.
I am sure the hon. Secretary of State would accept it, knowing that we will not get the bill by July 1. I am asking the Secretary of State to accept my proposal to the opposition. I hope we will stop being afraid for the future of the country. Of course we should respect the past, but we should build together and defend national unity. I ask hon. members to build national unity. I do not mean to suggest that they are antiCanadian or non-Canadian; I never want to be quoted as saying such.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in the two or three minutes remaining in the debate I want to make it clear that while I appreciate, fully understand and accept the sincerity of the words of the hon. member for
June 29, 1981

Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) who just sat down, I question this debate being brought on now on June 29, 1981, when the bill was introduced on June 19, 1980. We have had a whole year in which to consider this bill, but no, they must spring it on us.
The first time I heard about the bill was within the last couple of weeks. I heard that if the government could get a guarantee that it would pass through all stages with one speaker per side, then it would go through. Fine, it would be brought forward. If not, it would go on the back burner.

That is the way I heard the arrangements. This was the first part of the arrangements. Therefore, I am triply suspicious of the government's intentions. This is the third time in a fortnight when matters of this sort have been sprung upon us in a most extraordinary way.
The first occasion was approximately two weeks ago when out of the blue the government, for the second time in a decade, decided to have a debate on foreign affairs. We know what the government was doing. It was marking time because it was awaiting a ruling from the Supreme Court of Canada. The second time was when we dealt with CALURA. It was just a filler because the government was pulled up short on some of its estimates and realized it was in deep trouble. This time it is partly that and partly the fact the government is still floundering around, trying to make up its mind on how to deal with the $1.2 billion it was attempting to get illegally out of the House without anyone noticing it. Thank goodness someone noticed it. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) managed to bring it forward.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-SUMMER WORKS PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF APPLICATION DATE DEADLINE-DISSEMINATION OF INFORMATION
EMPLOYMENT-SUMMER WORKS PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF APPLICATION DATE DEADLINE-DISSEMINATION OF INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Government of Canada can afford to spend tens of millions of dollars on the advertising of those aspects of government policy which it wishes to sell to the public, it seems incredible to me that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) would suggest to me on April 3 that I, or any other member of Parliament, should be responsible for advertising the student employment program of this government. Perhaps the Minister of Employment and Immigration is not on good terms with the minister for propaganda. In that case, I recommend that he seek reconciliation prior to any program for winter employment so that Canada as a whole might be properly informed.
In a rural constituency it is virtually impossible to have any knowledge of all the people who might wish to apply for projects under make-work programs. If moneys are to be spent for advertising the various departments, it is imperative that

June 29, 1981
Adjournment Debate
some of it be spent for the general information of the public in a program which can mean so much to the small towns, villages and rural communities of Canada. At this particular time it would be interesting to know what the program for the winter is to be. What will be its name? What class of project will be eligible, and will there be any circulation of the terms and conditions of the program that rural Canadians may have an opportunity to apply for?
There is another aspect of the make-work programs which should be given some consideration. The accumulation of the statistics for the allocation of moneys is not done office by office in the employment and immigration structure. There is an accumulation of information which may be influenced by any part of the region concerned and may reflect very improperly upon other areas. For instance, in the economy of Carleton-Charlotte, as 1 pointed out last week, fishing, farming and forestry have been adversely affected by catastrophic interest rates and by the increase in the value of the Canadian dollar in respect of some foreign countries. This has brought about a reduction in the return of both raw and finished products which are exported from this constituency. And this constituency depends upon exports. The consequence of such a decline upon income may amount to as much as 24 per cent and as little as 10 per cent in some markets. The consequence of such a decline in income from exports for such an area is obvious even to an amateur economist.
Unfortunately, the nature of employment in Carleton-Char-lotte is seasonal. But the allocation of funds for make-work programs does not take this into consideration. Unless there is a very major turn-around in anticipated income, fishermen and fish processors will find themselves with a very low level of income this year and the unemployment figures along the coast of Carleton-Charlotte may reach an all-time high.
Can the minister advise me what particular consideration will be given when allocating winter works moneys for the unusual unemployment that will exist along the Bay of Fundy coast of Carleton-Charlotte? As an example, one processing plant in Campobello burned, and the economic climate is such that it will not be reconstructed in the near future. Will they get any special consideration for this?
In the rest of the fish processing industry, the indication is there will be less employment there as well. So will the Fundy coast get special consideration? Will the data accumulated from that area influence the moneys to be spent in that area? In the village of McAdam, the Georgia Pacific veneer plant has been closed, partly because of weakening of export markets and partly because there is virtually no housing program in Canada at all at this time. Furthermore, the CPR has withdrawn certain of its employment opportunities from McAdam and therefore there is a village of about 1500 people most of whom are unemployed.
Will this now be considered immediately in the accumulation of statistics for the allocation of make-works programs for this winter? I tried to get unemployment statistics which
would be applicable to the constituency and I am told they are just not available. However, those statistics which are accumulated in the individual offices of St. Stephens, Woodstock, Florenceville, etc., are put into the pool, and there is not, in fact, a reflection of those who are unemployed, those whose unemployment has expired, and those who have given up in the pursuit of work because there is no work available. But these figures which are publicized would indicate that we are more in line with the city of Fredericton than the city of Saint John in the employment rate, and this is not the case.
While I am quite prepared to acknowledge that there is a higher rate of employment in Carleton-Charlotte than there is in Gloucester or Westmorland-Kent, there is not that much difference that $3 million should have been allocated last winter for Gloucester, $3 million should have been allocated for Westmorland-Kent, and only $178,000 for Carleton-Charlotte, $100,000 for Fundy-Royal and $129,000 for York-Sun-bury. Yes, there is a difference, but not that much.
Would the minister consider meeting with members who have problems such as the one I have outlined, to determine a fashion in which allocation might be more rational, as they relate to the unemployment of the individual constituencies, rather than of a region, or of a half of New Brunswick, or whatever way this is put together? It would appear that Carleton-Charlotte will be little better off than Westmorland-Kent, for instance, in the coming winter, as far as employment is concerned.
I appeal to the minister through you, Your Honour, on behalf of the constituents of Carleton-Charlotte and other rural type constituencies which have been short-changed by virtue of a system which does not lend itself to the realities of employment opportunity any more than it would in rural P.E.I., rural Saskatchewan, or any other part of the country. There is no systematic accumulation of statistics which actually apply to any rural constituency in Canada. They are influenced by the cities we place around it.
