subtopic: MANPOWER-ONTARIO WOMEN'S OUTREACH GROUPS- REQUEST FOR MEETING WITH MINISTER
MANPOWER-ONTARIO WOMEN'S OUTREACH GROUPS- REQUEST FOR MEETING WITH MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 16. I questioned the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) concerning the very serious matters respecting the women's Outreach programs for projects in Ontario. The minister has refused eight times to meet with them. I understand that he still has not met with them personally.
I also raised the question of the very stringent regulations which have been implemented for member Outreach projects and the assimilation policy which is trying to centralize the very projects which were created to meet needs that could not be met in central offices; the frequent reviews that are imposed on these projects and the very-short term, three-month extensions which really in effect are killing Outreach projects across Canada.
I asked the minister about programs which are meeting permanent needs. In particular I mentioned the one with ethnic workers in Vancouver's Chinatown. These kind of permanent Outreach services should be funded in a permanent way as regular services and not simply as short-term projects.
The minister's answer was unsatisfactory. He gave no reply in response to the question about women's Outreach projects. I have checked Hansard and found that at least on four other occasions he has avoided this question in the House. He mentioned eight counselling units for women which have been established in manpower offices. While they may be valid services, they will not meet the kinds of special needs which Outreach projects are designed to meet. He talked about computerized job-finding services. This is a good idea and would be complementary to the Outreach service, but it would not replace Outreach in any way. He rationalized what appeared to be cutbacks that he would not admit by saying:
We are reallocating resources and targeting real needs.
Adjournment Debate
The real needs are for Outreach services funded in a permanent way. The values of Manpower Outreach programs for women and for other target groups have been demonstrated repeatedly. Successes are undisputed. In all evaluations, there is considerable documentation about how effective and how economical these services are.
There are 19 Outreach projects for women across Canada. These programs are all facing cutbacks and possible discontinuation. These projects have placed women in jobs. They have increased the number of opportunities for women who have traditionally been out of the labour force. They have provided employment counselling in store front kind of operations in neigbourhood communities. They have helped women who have been out of the labour force and who have little work experience to develop confidence and, new skills in seeking employment, and to keep jobs once they find them. They create support services and help women to have mutual support group sessions. They help them to find the needed child care. They help them to create training programs which are appropriate as well as to get into vocational services in the community.
There are many services provided in an Outreach way which cannot meet the needs of these women in the central offices of the manpower service. Perhaps those services are useful to meet the needs of the more motivated, confident and better educated women who are used to going into big bureaucracies and who know their way around the system. I cannot see them as being appropriate in the same way for older women who have been out of the work force and who lack confidence, or for immigrant women who do not know how to speak English well and do not know what the job market is in Canada, or for teenagers without experience or low-income women who have few skills and little education. These women need Outreach services.
I mentioned the Strathcona Manpower Outreach program which is another example of an essential service which should be funded permanently. It is located in downtown Chinatown in Vancouver. There are three workers who speak Cantonese. It attracts immigrants who do not speak English, immigrant workers who do not know their way around. They need a specific kind of help in their own language. These people know little about Canadian customs and the provisions under the labour code of Canada. They need counselling in their own language about the job situation, information and advice about Canadian customs and how to apply for jobs.
These people have the help of interpreters in filling out forms and getting around the city. As well, they have a very practical training program. For example, at Britannia Centre, a community school, they have set up a very practical program in the garment industry. The immigrants learn how to use Canadian machinery. They may not speak English, but they learn the technical English that is essential for their trade. They also have group sessions. Counsellors go into the English

June 29, 1981
Adjournment Debate
language classes and talk to them about resources. They also have a referral program operating.
This service has found jobs at a considerably higher rate per worker than the employment and immigration centres. They have found jobs in the garment industry, the hotel and restaurant industry, small businesses such as electronic firms and in fish canneries in Vancouver East. It has been a very worthwhile service, one that is very economical. Very little money has been spent on the bureaucracy. Most of it goes into direct service for clients.
Another Outreach service is the native Outreach program called NEED, Native Employment and Education Development. This is another downtown service in Gastown for native Indians, many of whom come from reserves to the city. They are quite lost when they do not have native people they know in a setting in which they feel comfortable. They go to the drop-in centre where they make friends and have native counsellors to tell them what is being offered.
All the services of the employment centre are decentralized and offered in their own setting. In this way they get access to programs. They get confidence building from Outreach and support services through that centre. It makes them feel confident when looking for jobs and in developing their potential. This service is needed.
I cannot see why the minister, with Treasury Board backing him, would not give high priority to continuing Outreach services. They are economically sound, effective in finding jobs, and help the employers in a much more practical way than central bureaucratic offices. They develop the potential of workers who have special needs and who cannot use the traditional Manpower offices. They create many supportive resources in the community.
Outreach services cost less and produce better results. The needs cannot be met through an assimilation project at the head office. Therefore I appeal to the minister and to Treasury Board: If funds must be cut, cut them from the central bureaucracies and keep the essential Outreach services that I have mentioned.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Henderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: MANPOWER-ONTARIO WOMEN'S OUTREACH GROUPS- REQUEST FOR MEETING WITH MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two separate issues which would appear to have been unfortunately combined in the present public discussions on the Outreach program. One is the policy review presently under way, and the other is the limited size of the program's budget and efforts that are being made to have it supplemented.
Perhaps I should deal with the budget first. The increase in the 1981-82 Outreach budget; as compared with the previous year, does not reflect the present rate of inflation. At the same time, the minister has been anxious to approve as many new projects as possible, particularly projects serving women. This has resulted in rather severe funding pressures on the program and more particularly on the budget of the Ontario region. As soon as this became apparent, efforts were initiated to indenti-fy any funds which might be available for transfer from other programs to Outreach. A decision from Treasury Board on this issue is expected shortly.
In the face of the severe funding limitations, however, the Ontario region was faced with only two alternatives: entering into 12-month contracts with projects for amounts of money which would reflect a decrease in activity compared with 1980-81; or entering into shorter term contracts for levels of activity which generally were consistent with previous activity levels, and relying on the success of the aforementioned efforts to find new money to enable the extension of the contracts at appropriate funding levels. This policy has not been limited to women's projects.
With respect to the second issue, that of future policy directions for Outreach, as with any government program, Outreach has been the subject of a review to determine how it might be improved and what, if any, new policy directions might be contemplated. The desirability for such a review results from a number of factors.
Once the minister has received the recommendations of his deputy minister as to the future role of Outreach, he will determine the nature of any consultations in which he may wish to be personally involved. He has instructed, however, that the analysis of all options reflect the results of the consultations now taking place.
As a final comment I would say that, contrary to some suggestions made in this House, the minister has not moved and is not moving to terminate either the Outreach program itself or Women's Outreach projects specifically. In fact, although final year-end expenditures for 1980-81 are not yet available, approximately $1,346,974, or 13.4 per cent of total Outreach program funds, went to projects serving women exclusively.
This represents an increase of 94.5 per cent over that expended in 1979-80, which was actually $692,567. I should
June 29, 1981

also point out that over 40 per cent of the clients of all Outreach projects serving all target groups are women. Further, the minister is actively seeking methods of supplementing the Outreach budget and, should additional funds become available, women's projects will continue to receive the highest priority.
